chapters.Chapitre 3 : Présentation technique du D: Lors de ce chapitre, nous allons exposer l’architecture technique et applicative de notre site, puis nous allons présenter la plateforme Hybris, ses fonctionnalités de base ainsi que les services qu'elle offre pour bien mener un site e-commerce. Finalement, nous allons citer les outils que nous avons utilisés pour la réalisation et pour l’établissement de notre usine logicielle. I. Architecture 1. Architecture d’ Hybris Commerce L'architecture de Hybris Commerce est flexible et modulaire, il est divisé en packages individuels, tels que le Commerce, le Content, le Channel et Order. Hybris Commerce contient plusieurs couches, chacune ayant une fonction différente et un niveau d'abstraction de données. Figure 13 : Architecture d’ Hybris 2. Architecture technique du Distrishop Hybris interagit avec différents systèmes et composants selon l’architecture suivante : Figure 14 : Architecture technique du Distrishop *VIP = Virtual IP address. Voir tableau 2 et tableau 3 du deuxième chapitre pour bien comprendre la définition de chaque composant. 3. Architecture de développement Le contrôleur récupère la requête HTTP envoyé par l’utilisateur, ensuite il fait appel à la façade pour invoquer le bon service qui à son tour fait appel au DAO pour récupérer les données d’Hybris. La façade envoie le modèle retourné par le service au convertisseur qui fait la conversion du modèle au DTO, ce dernier va être envoyé à nouveau à la façade pour l’envoyer au contrôleur. Ce DTO est l’objet de l’affichage sur la JSP. L’architecture ci-dessus permet d’avoir une indépendance entre les différentes couches, grâce à la façade qui nous permet de changer de la technologie tout en conservant le métier intact. Figure 15: Architecture de développement II. Plateforme Hybris Dans cette partie nous allons parler de la plateforme Hybris et plus précisément la version 6.3 de la plateforme. 1. Présentation de la plateforme Hybris Classée parmi les leaders dans les rapports Gartner Magic Quadrant for Marketing Resource choisie par Adidas, Reebok, Levi's, Toys"r"us, Nespresso, ainsi que plusieurs autres grandes marques commerciales. Racheté début juin 2013 par SAP, Hybris s’est vu bénéficier d’un nouvel élan de développement suite au versement d’importantes sommes de fonds par les investisseurs. Cette solution se prouve experte dans la gestion de grands catalogues et le multicanal. Offrant plusieurs « Accelerators » Prenant la forme de boutiques de démonstration (demonstration store), qui sont des sites clés en mains qui peuvent servir soit de démonstration ou être modifiés et adaptés aux besoins du client pour être mis en ligne en production. Ces fonctionnalités offertes par Hybris sont rassemblées dans des extensions qui rendent la plateforme 100% modulaires et extensible. Pour simplifier, Hybris est structuré comme suit : 1.1. Content Le contenu c’est l’essence des informations Core du site, plus spécialement les informations liées aux produits vendus, notamment :  Catalogues produits   Systèmes de classification et Catégories de produits   Médias (comme les images des produits etc ) 1.2. Orders Ce sont les Commandes. C’est la couche qui contient tous les détails liés aux commandes des produits incluant :  Promotions  Paiement et le processus de complétion  Gestion des inventaires  Gestion et historique des commandes  Détails des clients 1.3. Channel Channel réfère à comment on veut atteindre les clients. Ceci peut être fait à la fois par des méthodes physiques ou virtuelles comme :  Web store (interfaces Desktop et Mobile)  Kiosks et magasins  Les médias imprimés  Emails 1.4. Commerce Le composant Commerce apporte une collection de modules (fonctionnalités et options) dépendant du type de site commerce utilisé. Par défaut Hybris fournis deux types selon l’objectif du site : B2C (Business to Consumer) : B2C est pour les entreprises désirant vendre pour des individus, un site B2C a une panoplie d’options et vise à donner au client une méthode facile pour trouver, connaître et acheter les produits.  B2C (Business to Consumer) : B2C est pour les entreprises désirant vendre pour des individus, un site B2C a une panoplie d’options et vise à donner au client une méthode facile pour trouver, connaître et acheter les produits.  B2B (Business to Business) : B2B c’est pour quand une entreprise vise vendre ses produits pour d’autres entreprises. Ceci essentiellement concerne des commandes avec de très grandes quantités du même produit, avec des processus de communication et d’acceptation entre la plateforme et les systèmes de procuration. Il inclut aussi l’établissement des quotas et négociations potentielles sur les offres finalisées. 1.5. Platform C’est le dernier composant et le Core de la suite, c’est là où toute l’infrastructure réside et où se trouve l’interface de l’application. Hybris représente typiquement son architecture sous le format gâteau visible sur la figure. Figure 16 : Architecture générale de Hybris Commerce Suite SAP Hybris a été classé parmi les leaders du domaine par Gartner Magic Quadrant for Marketing Resource. Figure 17 : Classement Gartner Magic Quadrant for Marketing Resource Hybris a été classé parmi les leaders des solutions B2C dans The ForresterWave du Quartile 2 de 2017. Figure 18 : Classement the forresterwave Q2 2017 pour les solutions B2C 2. HybrisAccelerators Comme cité dans la présentation, Hybris offre de multiples Accelerators, sous formes de sites clés en main facilement personnalisables et prêts à être déployés, que ce soit pour le B2C ou le B2B. Ces sites sont des solutions de commerce omni-canal, avec des templates de storefronts complets et les outils métiers nécessaires pour la mise en place de n’importe quel type d’utilisation e-commerce. Plusieurs types d’Accelerators existent :  L’Accelerator B2C Electronics : site pour vente des produits électroniques (appareils photos etc )  L’Accelerator B2C Apparel : site pour vente des produits d’habillements et textile.  L’Accelerator B2C Telco : site pour vente des produits télécommunications (abonnements téléphoniques, téléphones etc ).  L’Accelerator B2B Power Tools : site pour vente des outils de travaux pour professionnels et c’est celui que nous utilisons dans ce projet. Tous ses sites sont fournis avec des données de bases pour les démonstrations et développement. 3. ImpEx Hybris Commerce Suite est livré avec une extension d'importation / exportation appelé ImpEx, c'est une interface entre les fichiers CSV et la plateforme Hybris. Cette extension permet de créer, mettre à jour, supprimer et exporter des éléments de la plateforme tel qu’un client, un produit, les données d'une commande à partir des fichiers CSV. Ces opérations peuvent être effectuées pendant l'exécution, l'initialisation ou la mise à jour du système. Durant l'élaboration de ce projet, nous avons utilisé les fichiers impex assez fréquemment, les champs de son utilisation sont nombreux, citons-nous quelques-uns :  Importer des données clients dans un système de production.  Synchroniser les données avec d'autres systèmes, comme un ERP.  Migrer des données d'une installation hybris vers une autre.  Peut être exécuté à partir des CronJobs. En gros, c'est une sorte d'abstraction de la base des données.Ci-dessous on trouve un exemple de syntaxe d'un fichier impex : marco $catalogVersion=catalogVersion(Catalog(id),version)[unique=true] header INSERT_UPDATE Product; code[unique=true]; name[lang=en]; unit(code);$catalogVersion comments #;;Samsung;;; values ;W580i;Sony Ericsson W580i; pieces; Default:Staged ;iphone5;Apple iphone 5; pieces; Default:Online Types of Modes: INSERT Product; code[unique=true]; name[lang=en]; unit(code); $catalogVersion UPDATE Product; code[unique=true]; name[lang=en]; unit(code); $catalogVersion Tout au long la réalisation de ce projet, nous utilisons souvent les fichiers impex vu leur importance dans la plateforme Hybris. 4. Les évolutions de la version 6.5 de Hybris 4.1. hMC vs Backoffice Parmi les points les plus remarquables dans la récente version de Hybris c’estl’intégration du module hMC (hybris Management Console) dans le module Backoffice cequi engendre l’élimination de l’interface hMC. D’abord, Le module hMC est l’interface graphique de l’utilisateur pour la plateforme Hybris. hMC est l’outil d’administration de la suite Hybris, exécuté dans un navigateur web. En l’utilisant, on peut gérer les différents objets d’Hybris, à savoir, les produits, les données des consommateurs, les commandes, etc L’interface hMC contient trois domaines majeurs, comme illustré dans la figure suivante : Figure 19 : Vue générale du HMC Le ToolbarhMC (1) en haut, l’arborescence à gauche (La navigation en hMC), ContentArea (2) au milieu et l’Explorer Tree (3) à gauche. Le Content Area affiche l’arborescence avec des icônes larges et des descriptions de chacune des entrées, comme le montre la figure Il peut être utilisé comme une interface avec trois éléments majeurs (Search Area, Result Area, et Editor Area). Le dernier backoffice nommé simplement « Backoffice » représente la troisième et dernière génération d’interface d’administration. Il vise à remplacer le HMC ainsi que les cockpits, néanmoins toutes les fonctionnalités des anciens backoffices ne sont pas encore implémentées, il garde presque la même structure d’arborescence que le hMC. Actuellement, les objets Hybris sont administrables depuis le Backoffice comme illustré ci- dessous : Figure 20 : Vue générale du Backoffice 4.2. Accelerator B2C versus Accelerator B2B Dans les versions antérieures, on faisait forcément une séparation entre les deux accélérateurs B2C et B2B, mais à partir de la version 6 de Hybris, on se basait sur le contenu de la version initiale générée à base d'accélérateur B2C plus les Add-ons B2B pour avoir une solution B2B. III. Outils et technologies utilisés Mis à part l’outil principal Hybris décris auparavant, nous avons utilisé les outils et technologies suivantes dont quelques-unes sont intégrées dans le "out-of-the box" de la plateforme Hybris (Spring, Web services ). 1. Environnements de développement et outils Eclipse Eclipse est un environnement de développement intégré (IDE) hautement extensible. Son objectif est de produire et fournir des outils pour la réalisation de logiciels ; il englobe les activités de programmation, de modélisation, de conception, de testing, de gestion, de configuration, reporting, etc Jira Comme expliqué lors du deuxième chapitre, les exigences de client seront intégrées sur JIRA afin que les développements soient surveillés en temps réel par tous les acteurs du projet De plus, la surveillance de la 'vélocité' et le 'BurndownChart' nous permettront d'anticiper toute déviation et de prendre les mesures appropriées. Confluence Confluence est un logiciel de rédaction des contenus et de partage des informations. Organisé dans des zones appelées "spaces" qui contiennent des pages de contact, des pièces jointes et d'autres types de contenu pouvant être visualisés et édités par les utilisateurs. Les spécifications de client sont rédigées sur Confluence, le Product Owner a accès en mode lecture et peut ajouter des commentaires sur certaines parties de la spécification pendant le processus de validation. Git Git est un logiciel de gestion de versions décentralisé, il ne repose pas sur un serveur centralisé. C'est un outil de bas niveau, qui se veut simple et performant, dont la principale tâche est de gérer l'évolution du contenu d'une arborescence. C'est le remplaçant de SVN dans la première version de la forge logicielle. Il a été adopté pour son efficacité dans le travail collaboratif, notamment par l'apport des plugins tels que git-flow (voir figure ci-dessous) qui rationalise le cycle des livraisons (releases) en utilisant des branches séparées pour le développement de fonctionnalités, la préparation des livraisons, et la maintenance. Dans notre cas, GIT est géré par le logiciel gitLab côté serveur et sourceTree côté client. 2. Frameworks utilisées JEE La technologie Java Entreprise Edition (JEE) définit la norme de développement des applications d’entreprise distribuées et multi tiers. Elle permet de simplifier les applications d'entreprise en se basant sur des composants modulaires normalisés tout en fournissant un ensemble complet de services et en gérant automatiquement un grand nombre de détails sur le Spring Spring est un Framework libre pour construire et définir l'infrastructure d'une application java, il facilite le développement et les tests. Il est nommé un conteneur dit “ léger ”, c’est-à-dire une infrastructure similaire à un serveur d'applications JEE. Il prend donc en charge la création d’objets et la mise en relation d’objets par l’intermédiaire d’un fichier de configuration qui décrit les objets à fabriquer et les relations de dépendances entre eux. Le grand avantage, par rapport aux serveurs d’application, c’est qu’avec Spring, les classes n’ont pas besoin d’implémenter une quelconque interface pour être prises en charge par le Framework (au contraire des serveurs d'applications JEE). Web Service La technologie des services Web est un moyen rapide de distribution de l'information entre clients, fournisseurs, partenaires commerciaux et leurs différentes plates-formes. Les services Web sont basés sur le modèle SOA, ils communiquent via un ensemble de technologies fondamentales qui partagent une architecture commune comme HTTP, WSDL, REST, SOAP ainsi de suite Lors de ce projet, nous avons utilisé l'architecture REST pour la récupération des données depuis SAP, cette architecture repose sur le protocole HTTP en accédant à une ressource via différentes opérations (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) et en se basant sur le format JSON comme format d'échange. IV. Conclusion Dans ce chapitre nous avons exposé l’architecture de notre site, comment nous avons séparé les différentes parties et comment elles interagissent. Nous avons aussi présenté les fonctionnalités les plus importantes de la plateforme Hybris. Puis nous avons clôturé le chapitre par une présentation des technologies utilisées et l’usine logicielle que nous avons mise en place pour la réalisation de ce projet

Figure 35 : Cas demande déja enregistrer Pour la réalisation de ce traitement nous avons réalisé les deux coté (back & front),pour le coté back nous avons ajouté un nouveau item AMDSProductBackInStock qui contient deux attributs (Product Code) (Customer Code) afin d’enregistrer les demandes. Après nous avons ajouté un contrôleur qui permet de réalisé la vérification de demande pour l’utilisateur pour un produit demandé d’une part, et l’enregistrement d’une nouvelle demande d’autre part. Pour le coté front nous avons réalise la partie de traitement Ajax afin de gérer les différent cas citer précédemment. 5. Le processus de check-out Cette fonctionnalité se fait l’une des fonctionnalités les plus cruciales dans le Distrishop car elle contient le processus de la passation d’une commande. 5.1. Problématique Le défi que nous avons rencontré pendant la mise en œuvre de cette partie est d’une part, celui des régressions suite à la modification des données de « PowerTools » lors des itérations précédentes ce qui nous a empêchés de passer une commande avec succès. D’une autre part, l’éloignement des spécifications du client de ce qu’offre l’accélérateur d’Hybris dans cette étape. 5.2. Solution Pour remédier à ce problème, nous avons récupéré les données de l’accélérateur PowerTools d’une façon temporaire.Pour la confirmation un email envoyé au client contient les détails de leur commande. Figure 36 : Les étapes de la création d'une commande dans le Distrishop 6. Gestion du contenu CMS La partie CMS prend une partie cruciale dans ce projet, lors de cette itération nous avons procédé par la création d'un ensemble des pages CMS et qu'elles-mêmes et leur contenu sont administrables depuis le backoffice, nous nous sommes basés sur une template crée par des fichiers impex. En général, on suit le processus suivant pour qu'on obtienne le résultat souhaité Figure 37 : Processus de la création d'une page CMS Un exemple parmi les contenu CMS qui nous avons ajouté, le composant (13) créer via impex par l’ajout d’un CMSParagraphComponentLier à une « content slot » cette dernier lier à une « ContentSlotForPage » 7. Gestion Mon entreprise Figure 38 : Mon entreprise Les fonctionnalités de gestion d'organisation d'hybris Commerce Accelerator pour B2B permettent aux entreprises de faire des achats en libre-service via le site Web B2B Accelerator d'un marchand. Les entreprises peuvent créer plusieurs organisations (ou unités appelées dans B2B Accelerator), qui sont ensuite associées aux utilisateurs, aux groupes d'utilisateurs, aux seuils de commande, aux budgets et aux centres de coûts. Les fonctionnalités de gestion d'organisation sont accessibles via la page Mon entreprise de l'accélérateur B2B, qui est ensuite divisée en plusieurs sections :  Budgets  Centres de coûts  Unités d'affaires  Utilisateurs  Groupes d'utilisateurs  Autorisations de commande  Relevé de compte Seuls les utilisateurs auxquels le rôle Administrateur B2B a été attribué peuvent accéder aux fonctionnalités de l'organisation. 7.1. Problématique la page mon entreprise existe dans les ancien version de l'Accelerator "PowerTools" Hybris , mais d'une façon statique . Il est demandé de créer la page mon entreprise et qui contient des composants dynamiques liés à chaque fonctionnalités de la page mon entreprise et intégrer un style unique selon le type de devise connecté (Bureau,Tablet,Mobile) 7.2. Solution Figure 39 : point d'acces page Mon entreprise Les liens réels différeront en fonction du rôle de l'utilisateur et d’autres facteurs. Dans l'exemple précédent, l'utilisateur est un administrateur B2B, l'icône Mon Entreprise est donc visible. Pour appliquer ce traitement il faut récupère les droits de l’utilisateur et vérifier que le droit d’administrateur B2B existe. Pour la création de la page mon entreprise, nous avons ajouté tout d’abord dans l’impex un composant JspIncludeComponent qui a une référence vers une page jsp que nous avons créé après, nous avons lié ce composant a une contentSlot cette dernier lier à une ContentSlotForPage. Apres l’import de ce impex , nous avons créé un contrôleurs qui permet d’accéder à la page mon entreprise une fois la page est apparaisse , nous avons améliorer les différentes méthodes dans le contrôleur pour pouvoir récupéré les différentes information visible dans la page suivant leur définition dans le cahier de charge. III. Etat d’avancement et prespective 1. Etat actuel Nous sommes maintenant arrivés à 80% du projet, la majorité des fonctionnalités majeures requises se sont réalisées dans les trois sprints achevés. Juste après la livraison de la troisième itération et avant de commencer le développement des fonctionnalités de la quatrième itération, nous avons dédié toute une itération qu’on avait appelé « Sprint de stabilisation » pour la stabilisation du Distrishop et aussi pour traiter les nouvelles demandes de modification prioritaires à notre client. En principe, il ne nous reste que les parties suivantes : « Mon entreprise » qui contient toutes les pages concernant les informations de l’organisation d’un client AMDS ainsi que le mécanisme de la vérification du stock d’un produit. Ces fonctionnalités sont incluses dans la quatrième itération qui était entamée durant la rédaction de cette partie de notre mmoire, cette itération serait la dernière itération avant la première mise en ligne (GoLive) de la version v1.0 de notre Distrishop pour ensuite entamer la discussion des fonctionnalités à ajouter et à modifier dans la prochaine version. 2. Les tests Les tests unitaires, les tests croisés et les tests de non régression sont effectués par l’équipe de test qui fait partie de l’équipe AMDS d’Oujda. Ces tests sont effectués en parallèle avec le développement et pendant les derniers jours avant la livraison du sprint et après avoir fait le « 3. Déploiement Notre Distrishop est déployé dans trois environnements à savoir :  DEV01 : C’est l’environnement de test de SQLI.  UAT01 : C’est l’environnement de test de notre client ArcelorMittal (pré-production)  PROD : C’est l’environnement de production. Afin que notre équipe de test puissent faire ses tests d’une façon quotidienne et en temps réel le site est mis dans la PIC_SQLI, une usine de développement de SQLI tel que :  APP1 et APP2 ainsi que leurs bases de données sont à Rabat.  APP3 et APP4 ainsi que leurs bases de données sont à Oujda. 4. Perspectives Ce projet, étant le premier projet Hybris à SQLI Oujda, dans une perspective proche d’être présenté aux clients du groupe comme la première plateforme e-commerce B2B d’ArcelorMittal qui les permettra de faire le e-merchandising en commençant par leur agence de Toulouse en France. Ceci dans l’objectif de mesurer la satisfaction du client vis-à-vis ce Distrishop et qui va par la suite permettre SQLI Oujda de réaliser des versions ultérieures du Distrishop et aussi inclure toutes les autres agences du client en Europe pour qu’elles aient une plateforme e-commerce B2B permettant SQLI Oujda de poursuivre son activité d’Hybris IV. Conclusion  Lors de ce chapitre, j’ai expliqué le processus de développement des exigences du client en adaptant la méthodologie Scrum et en respectant les principes de développement d’Hybris ainsi que les normes de codage du Java afin de livrer un produit performant et de qualité. Vers la fin de ce chapitre, nous avons décrit l’état actuel, et ce qui reste à faire en termes de fonctionnalités et les perspectives et objectifs à atteindre après la réalisation de ce Distrishop

general_introduction: Social responsibility has evolved beyond charity and volunteers to cover responses to society’s economic, social, and environmental challenges. University social responsibility (USR) has ac- quired prominence in the European higher education setting. At the same time, while the expansion of private and public institutions promotes educational progress and contributes to a bright national future, it also increases energy demand. The fun- damentalproblemisthatmostinstitutionsconsumealotofenergy,whichrequiresthemtomake substantial rehabilitation and renovation efforts, leading to very high financial costs. Article 175 of the ELAN law has introduced the implementation of an ambitious energy improvement program in the code of construction and housing the obligation. Specifically, as an example, the decree tertiary of July 23, 2019, indicates that the reduction of final energy consumption of these buildings will have to reach at least 40% in 2030 and 50% in 2040 compared to 2010. Thisistoencourage, amongotherthings, establishmentstoconsumelessandbetter. Toachieve the reduction scenario envisaged by the State of a 10% reduction every ten years until 2050, it is necessary to install a periodic monitoring protocol. The added value of this internship project lies in the original implementation of a dynamic energy management protocol (DEMP) with 4 phases, 3 of which are consecutive and periodic and one dedicated to research and in- vestigation. The first three phases of DEMP are 1-Audit phase or data collection of all energy expenses, 2-Analysis of the data and 3-Implementation of the improvement strategy about the policy of the institution and the funds it has. DEMP aims to empower universities to optimize their energy management. If phases 2- and 3- can be handled relatively easily internally, phase one of the audit is more critical. Indeed, the precise mapping of the energy expenses of a university like Pau is challenging to obtain for various reasons: its size, diversity of buildings, diversity of the types of heating and locations But the systematic and periodic recourse to a specialized research department would be too expensive, too rigid and not sufficiently ef- fective over time. Hence the interest in the original implementation of this protocol, even if thefirstauditwillrequirethehelpofaspecializedconsultingfirmtoinitiatetheDEMPprocess. The USR initiative at UPPA attempts to establish an institutional policy that recognizes the university’s responsibilities to society and the environment. UPPA aims to support the CSD- MBC: Climate and Sustainable Development - Mentality and Behavior Change in the spirit of CSR for businesses and uses the relevant section of the ISO26000 standard as a reference. The UPPA University Social ResponsibilitY system is modeled after the physical paradigm of matter. The UPPA URS atom is at its center, and four phases orbit around it like electrons. The symbolism of this depiction is intriguing for two reasons: as with physics, this model eluci- dates a difficulty, not the least of which is the concept of infinitely big to infinitely small scales. We shall discover it can be divided into four distinct periods. The first phase discusses UPPA’s social responsibility in its current state. The second phase entails developing an action plan It is critical to keep in mind that any social responsibility project (in this case, in four phases) is cyclical and never-ending. Thus, phase one of the inventory must be repeated over time at a predetermined frequency specified by the numerous advancements accomplished. Any modification to phase one will undoubtedly result in modifications to phases 2, 3, and 4
general_conclusion: This work demonstrates that all occupations and professions in higher education and research institutionscanandmustcontributetoachievingtheSDGsthroughenhancedinter-disciplinary collaboration. Given the environmental and socioeconomic issues of the 21st century, everyone of us is re- sponsible for acting through voting, daily conduct, citizenship, and professional engagement. However, in the professional realm, action for sustainable development and social responsibility is frequently reduced to environmentally-friendly gestures and awareness-raising activities, and appears to be limited to specific specialized occupations. Nonetheless, profound change is required to address the environmental and social problems we face: change that will affect how we report and communicate, how we advise and support students, teaching and research methodologies, risk management and end-user protection, and our international interactions. In addition, each of these components is supported by HEI pro- fessions whose activities are directly related to SD&SR. To this end, we must: (cid:136) Define the social issues and potential contributions of each HEI profession; (cid:136) Show how we are all affected by the SDGs and how each higher education professional can make a difference with his or her function and experience; (cid:136) Inspire contemplation about how social issues may influence the progress of professions; (cid:136) Learn how professions with similar social concerns collaborate and how to form new associations. The SDGs constitute a new global cause. Despite covering a vast array of topics, they are user-friendly. The seventeen goals are a list of the most pressing challenges of our day. Defining them as objectives provides a framework for addressing these difficulties. The goals are also the best instrument for examining the aforementioned needs. Onapersonallevel,theproductionofthisprojectwasquiteenlightening,asallreferenceshadto be uncovered and analyzed. The concepts that I was able to create throughout my internship contributed coherence and adaptability to my training, both in terms of comprehending an audit strategy and developing subject-specific indicators. In addition, through understanding the implications of the concept of social responsibility. Thus, the many missions allowed me to strengthen and broaden my scientific knowledge and culture. The fact that I am constantly surrounded by knowledgeable individuals who listen to me allows me to expand my technical knowledge and motivates me to continue my education. This internship has exceeded my expectations completely. Glossary Art. 55 of the Grenelle I Environment Act Article 55 of Law N. 2009-967 of August 3, 2009 on the implementation of the Grenelle de l’environnement, also known as ”Grenelle 1,” requires all institutions of higher education to implement a sustainable development approach through a Green Plan and to be eligible to apply for a label based on sustainable development criteria. 57 Grenelle I law The Grenelle I Act, or Act No. 2009-967 of August 3, 2009 on the implemen- tation of the Grenelle Environment Forum, is a French programming law that formalizes the 268 commitments of the Grenelle Environment Forum. 56 Sustainable development A guiding principle for achieving human development objectives while preserving the capacity of natural systems to supply the natural resources and ecosystem services upon which the economy and society depend. 46 The Green Plan In 2010, a mechanism called a reference system was developed by the Con- ference of University Presidents, the Conference of Grandes Ecoles, the FNSSD, and the Ministry of Ecological Transition to implement the Green Plan. With cooperation from the Ministry of Higher Education, Research, and Innovation, its most recent version was suggested in 2021. 56 The International Organization for Standardization ISO is an international organiza- tion for the development of standards comprised of delegates from the national standards organizations of its member nations. 43 The law on higher education and research The law of 22 July 2013 is a law of openness (to the socio-economic environment, the international scene, and all types of teaching and research) and a law of transformation. Its common threads are student achievement and a new research goal. 56

chapters.Chapter 1: General context of the project Introduction Theoretically, no action should be undertaken without a thorough understanding of the human or economic environment into which the project will intervene. Hence, this chapter summarizes our final year project’s working environment and objectives. We begin by introducing the research and academic environment of the host organization, “The University of Pau and the Adour countries, SIAME Laboratory.” Second, the following section will outline our project’s framework, context, and objectives. 1.1 The University of Pau and the Pays de l’Adour The UPPA has its origins in a local university history that dates all the way back to the XVIth century, with the establishment of a Coll`ege des Arts (a humanities institute) in 1549 and then the third protestant academy in Europe in 1564, which was renamed a University in 1583. When the B ́earn region was incorporated into France in 1620, the University was abolished. In 1722, a new Universitas Bearniae was founded. It began with a Faculty of Arts and Humanities and a Faculty of Law before adding a Faculty of Theology in 1780. This university ceased to exist in 1792, during the French Revolution. In 1809, France was divided into academic regions as part of the creation of the Napoleonic University system, and Pau became the seat of an academicregion, coveringtheBassesPyr ́en ́ees(today’sPyr ́en ́eesAtlantiques), HautesPyr ́enees and Landes areas (or d ́epartements). In 1848, the Second Republic ended this division (?). The UPPA is then created in several steps from 1946 to 1970. Figure 1.1: General organization of UPPA 1.1.2 Political organization chart Figure 1.2: Political organization chart 1.1.3 A university of excellence serving a territory The University of Pau and the Pays de l’Adour is one of only a few French universities to bear the I-SITE (Ini- tiatives Science, Innovation, Territories, and Economy) la- bel. The University of Pau and the Pays de l’Adour (UPPA) received the ”Investissement d’avenir” label for two reasons: it is recognized as an exceptional university through the E2S UPPA project, Solutions for Energy and the Environment, led by the UPPA, INRA, Inria, and CNRS consortium (I-SITE label), and through the SPACE project, Progressive and Accompanied Specialization of Student Curricula (NCU label, New University Courses). Multidisciplinary and multisite, UPPA benefits from an exceptional working environment on five campuses on a human scale: Pau, Bayonne, Anglet, Mont-de-Marsan and Tarbes. The UPPA prepares more than 13,500 students to obtain a hundred or so degrees from Bac+1 to Bac+8 in law, economics, management, literature, languages, human sciences, sport, science and technology. With 19 research units, 34 high-level expertise chairs and nine standard labs in association with major research organizations (CNRS, INRAe, Inria) and institutional and industrial partners, UPPA is a significant player in the scientific and economic development of southern Aquitaine. Thanks to its international cooperation, UPPA is also active at the European level with the Eu- ropean Universities Label for the UNITA project, Universitas Montium, which brings together, in addition to UPPA, the universities of Turin (Italy), Savoie Mont Blanc and Covilha ̃-Beira (Portugal), Timisoara Ouest (Romania) and Zaragoza (Spain), which is in addition to the EDENE project (European Doctoral Programme in Energy and Environment), which allows the financing of 30 international doctoral students in the field of Energy and Environment and partnership with several local industrial players. 1.1.4 Research in UPPA The University of Pau and Pays de l’Adour (UPPA) has defined two values that guide its research activity: a. reconciling science and society for a sustainable progress b. acting within a territory. For the period 2022-2026, these values are expressed in five interdisciplinary missions focused on societal issues. Ex- pressed in a language that the most significant number of people can understand, these missions are intended to en- compass all the stakeholders in the region around the UPPA teams. five missions are : “Organizing energy subsidiarity at the territorial scale” “Re-assessing borders and rising up to the Mission challenge of differences” Mission “Reconciling “Resilience research and development with a safe and adaptation of the coastal, forest and environment and a preserved biodiversity” mountain ecosystems” Mission Mission The mission ”Representations and construction of tomorrow’s territories” The SIAME laboratory is a host team of the University of Pau and Pays de l’Adour, whose research is carried out in the field of Engineering Sciences. The unit is structured into four teams: (cid:136) Complex flows and Energetics (EE), (cid:136) Geomaterials and Civil Engineering Structures (GS), (cid:136) Interaction Waves / Structures (IVS), (cid:136) High Voltage Processes (PHT). The research is based on practical expertise, modeling, and numerical simulations. The labora- toryisamemberoftheresearchfederationsIPRAandMIRAandtheCarnotInstituteISIFOR. One of the significant assets of the laboratory is its historical partnership activity, which is reflected in the participation of its teams in three joint laboratories (SAGE, KOSTARISK and UPPA-Nobatek/INEF4). The research themes developed within the SIAME laboratory are part of two of the four main research fields structuring research at the institutional level, notably through membership of these two federations: Field 1: Energy and Territories. The laboratory contributes to field 1 through the thermo- physical characterization of materials associated with the storage of thermal energy and the optimization of sustainable energy systems (Team EE), and the implementation of high fre- quency and high power electrical energy conversion devices (Team PHT), Field 2: Ecosystems, biodiversity and secure development. In this field, the research developed at SIAME concerns the control of coastal risks (Team IVS), the development of bio-sourced and geo-sourced eco-building materials, and technical-environmental optimization (Team GS). Figure 1.3: ORGANIZATIONAL CHART 2022 - Engineering Sciences Applied to Mechanical and Electrical Engineering (SIAME) The subject is a component of the UPPA’s UnisVerts5Cit ́es social responsibility project (see. UnisVerts5Cit ́es: Towards an eco-citizen university, the UPPA’s response to the difficulties of sustainable development. Numerous actions or subjects can be proposed to the learner based on his or her interests. Each of the proposed topics includes a publishable portion in the sense of research and a portion that is freely usable by others. Regardless of the social responsibility plan chosen by the institution, the audit of the latter is one of the first steps and remains essential. Based on a document issued by the CPU (Conference of University Presidents, now France Universities) and intended for all higher education institutions, the questionnaire for this audit highlights 16 families of RSE activities concerningthe17UNsustainabledevelopmentobjectives. Afirststep, andnottheleast, ofthis audit, has already been carried out at UPPA since the different departments of the institution have already answered. First of all, the proposed work consists of the analysis of the results to integrate them into the implementation of a dynamic ADHU audit protocol intended for RSEs. In a second step, after publication of this protocol in the appropriate journal, it will be proposed to all universities in France. 1.3.1 Context and framework of the project The University Social Responsibility project is aligned with the UniVerts5Cit ́es campaign, which was introduced and launched on the UPPA website a few years ago and continues to this day. In a setting of humanitarian and ecological catastrophe that is getting more and more concerning, it becomes imperative to warn the populace and educate them on the steps they need to take to combat the impending changes as soon as possible. This project will first seek to establish a mental organization that will structure its application at the university. chapters.Chapter 3: The state of the art: USR in UPPA Introduction Different economic, political, and social transformations have occurred in the university sector over the past three decades, resulting in a comprehensive overhaul to meet the new societal issues these institutions face today. This highlights the social aspect of colleges and their vital function as educators of future leaders and policymakers. This demonstrates the necessity for institutions to integrate social responsibility ideas into their core operations. Social responsibility is a responsibility, not a requirement, of an organization for the impact of its decisions and activities on society and the environment, through transparent and ethical behavior that contributes to sustainable development, health, and the welfare of society; that takes into account the expectations of stakeholders, complies with applicable law and is consis- tent with international norms of behavior; and that is integrated throughout the organization. Universities can demonstrate their commitment to social responsibility through the promotion of sustainable development strategies in higher education institution administration. It should be integrated into the university’s ideology as a way of being, operating, and conducting busi- ness. Universities should infuse social responsibility into their basic beliefs and functions at every level. 3.1 Corporate Social Responsibility Globally, social responsibility (SR) has grown in prominence, and it has gotten entwined in the debate over competitiveness and sustainability in the context of globalization (Vasilescu et al., 2010).Social responsibility is a broad notion that encompasses all forms of business. It is a well-known business theory that is not limited to companies by definition. The term ”social responsibility” refers to legal and ethical obligations resulting from an organization’s operations’ influence on society, economy, and environment. Universities are also accountable for the influence of their actions on various stakeholder groups (e.g., students, staff, professors, alumni, and local communities). As centers of knowledge, universities must provide an ethical example by assuring equitable operating systems, transparency, and adherence to human rights (Gomez, 2014). The World Business Council for Sustainable development provides a commonly used definition of SR as follows: ” Corporate social responsibility is the continuing commitment by business to behave ethically and contribute to economic development while improving the quality of life of the workforce and their families as well as of the local community and society at large.” (CSR: Meeting Changing Expectations, 1999). CSR is defined by the company’s ethical behavior and transparency toward all of its stakeholders, as well as by the establishment of cor- social problem reduction (Sousa Filho et al., 2010). CSR is a long-term commitment to ethical behavior and economic growth while enhancing the well-being of people and the environment. It’s a new way of conducting business that involves corporations responding to stakeholders about operations that influence the economy, society, and environment in either a good or bad way (Gomez, 2014). The World Business Council for Sustainable Development defined CSR as more proactively and multi-stakeholder. CSR demonstrates a sustained multistakeholder commitment since it considers not just the workforce’s (workers’) quality of life but also their families, local communities, and society, contributing to economic progress (Moir, 2001). It also describes the connection between businesses and society (Porter and Kramer, 2006). However, CSR practice and its ramifications cannot be extended to higher education institutions. USR differs from CSR in that it considers specific effects that businesses are unaware of and unique characteristics that well-known rules do not (Vallaeys et al., 2009).As a result, corporations and universitieshavedistinctperspectivesonsocialresponsibilityandwhatitentails(Gomez,2014). The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) defined CSR following the consen- sus of a multistakeholder working group from several countries throughout the world. ISO 26000 in Social Responsibility, a practical framework for any organization’s social responsibil- ity practices, was presented and published by ISO in 2011. One of the working groups’ initial responsibilities was to agree on a concept of social responsibility: Organizational accountability for the effects of its decisions on society and the environment through transparent and ethical behavior that: contributes to sustainable development, in- cluding health and social welfare; considers stakeholder expectations; complies with applicable law and international standards of behavior; and is integrated throughout the organization’s relationships (Borealis, 2011 citing ISO 2010, clause 2.18, p.3). CSR can have several distinguishing characteristics, including sound governance, social and environmental repercussions management, interaction and communication with critical stake- holders, and collaboration with other organizations to achieve sustainable development (Val- laeys et al., 2009). There are numerous benefits (direct and indirect) associated with CSR practice. One of these benefits is enhancing relationships with stakeholders and recruiting qualified people keen to work for socially responsible businesses, fostering positive and attitude-changing behaviors among various stakeholder groups (Marinoff et al., 2014). CSR practices have evolved into a critical component of firms’ daily agendas worldwide. Busi- nesses have begun to operate more responsibly, embracing social and environmental initiatives. However, businessesshouldbemindfulthatsimplypromotingCSRpracticesisinsufficient; they must effectively communicate CSR both internally and externally to all categories of stakehold- ers (Marinoff et al., 2014). As a result, organizations that promote social and environmental activities can elicit favorable responses from various stakeholders (?). CSR communication can be defined as disseminating knowledge about economic, social, and environmental actions. It must be relevant and exciting to stimulate an interchange of ideas that results in new per- spectives, collaborations, and even changes in behaviors and attitudes among companies and stakeholders. unanticipated consequences (Vallaeys et al., 2009). For example, educational and cognitive impacts contribute to resolving pedagogical and epistemological issues that are unique to uni- versities and not to businesses (Vallaeys et al., 2009). As a result, corporations and colleges approach social responsibility differently (both in theory and practice). 3.2 The Concept of Sustainable Development and Its Relationship with Corporate Social Responsibility- Review of the Scientific Literature The term ”sustainable development” was coined in 1987 by the United Nations World Com- mission on Environment and Development in its report ”Our Common Future.” It refers to a process that ”meets the requirements of the present without jeopardizing future generations’ ability to fulfill their own needs” (Dahlsrud, 2008). While developing an effective strategy for achieving sustainable development, the three primary areas listed below should be considered (Freeman and Hasnaoui, 2011). (cid:136) Nature conservation and resource management (e.g., pollution reduction, protection of endangered plant and animal species, and promotion of renewable energy sources); (cid:136) economic growth and equitable distribution of profits (e.g., facilitating developing coun- tries’ access to markets, funding development, and altering irrational patterns of con- sumption and production); (cid:136) social advancement (e.g., combating poverty and access to education and health protec- tion). The concept of sustainable development, which emphasizes the importance of considering so- cial and environmental aspects of business activity and the economic dimension, is viewed as a critical factor in determining an organization’s interest in developing a socially responsible business model. As a result, corporate social responsibility is incorporated into the concept of sustainable development (CSR). As a result, corporate social responsibility is incorporated into the concept of sustainable development (CSR). CSR should be viewed as the management’s obligation to make decisions and take activities that benefit both their own interests and the protection and expansion of social well-being. Social responsibility is defined as ”the practice of going above and beyond legal requirements (commitments) to achieve a successful balance of obligations to investors, customers, other businesses, and other communities”. The fulfillment of auxiliary obligations is a significant aspect of social responsibility. This includes, but is not limited to, respect for the interests of organization stakeholders, such as adherence to human rights, appropriate protection of customers and development of products with their needs in mind, contribution to the creation of well-being, creation of workplaces, concern for workers and their families, concern for the natural environment, and adherence to legal regulations and ethical principles (Kiez ̇el et al., 2021). CSR is predicated on several critical assumptions. Business and society are components of a broader whole. The concept of mutual solidarity between people is paramount, and the strategic business objective is to contribute to the growth of prosperity and enhancement of citizens’ quality of life. To ensure their long-term viability, firms are driven by the dynamic nature of the social system to adopt social behaviors that are primarily preventative and risk- averse. The bare minimum level of economic and legal corporate responsibility is established by the requirements of a community at a particular stage of social development. Each action taken by an enterprise that demonstrates concern for the consumer, its employees, and the natural environment; goes beyond the bare minimum level of ethical responsibility required by law; and complies with community expectations contributes to the enterprise’s competitiveness in the market. The enterprise’s level and breadth of social responsibility are represented in its structural and organizational readiness to achieve social goals aligned with the demands and expectations of target markets. 3.3 University Social Responsibility Concept Universities cannot remain disconnected from current thinking on social responsibility and sus- tainable development, implemented in numerous businesses over the last few years (Va ́zquez et al., 2016). Universities are a critical component of any society. Over the last decades, numerous economic, political, and social changes have occurred in the university sector, ne- cessitating considerable reform to address these institutions’ societal issues in their primary activities (Vasilescu et al., 2010). One could argue that the role of universities in the modern world has gone beyond the fundamental assumption of knowledge generation and distribution. Academics and practitioners have discussed the role of a higher education institution to meet individual and societal requirements (Ali et al., 2021). The volume of literature continues to grow as scholars from other disciplines learn about the contributions of HEIs in a variety of fields and disciplines (Ali et al., 2021). Additionally, the last few decades’ worldwide economic, social, political, and technological transformations have profoundly affected the educational sector, notably higher education and opment, and software development, in addition to a growing emphasis on market forces as one of the significant factors influencing the very identity of universities and their organization (Vasilescu et al., 2010).Universities are accountable for their influence on various stakehold- ers through their activities (e.g., students, staff, alumni, and outside the community). As instructive organizations, universities must adhere to their responsibility of supporting moral and ethical principles, establishing norms for appropriate workplace solutions, openness, and respect for human rights. Universities play a unique role in establishing a sustainable future, as the development and diffusion of information and its application is a primary issue (Esfijani and Chang, 2012). Universities have a responsibility to develop socially responsible human resources equipped with knowledge and ethical behavior. Today’s average student is becoming more proactive due to social media and online communities that affect and strengthen their capacities to assess and implement activities that promote personal and societal fulfillment (Belyaeva et al., 2018). The scope of USR operations performed by institutions under various pretexts to address the severity of issues encountered is depicted in 3.1. As social responsibility pertains to an organization’s economic, legal, altruistic, and moral responsibilities, institutions of higher education are required to go above and beyond their fundamental responsibilities of developing students, conducting research, and engaging in com- munity outreach, and to align these activities with the concept of USR (Ali et al., 2021). While educational institutions are loud about their social conscience, any institution is prone to un- desirable social consequences if unaware of its fundamental social mission (Su et al., 2018). At the turn of the twenty-first century, universities were forced to rethink their role and status in society. The literature analysis established substantial and sustainable practices in various academic settings (Hosny et al., 2013). Most universities in today’s world are conscious of their ecological impact and have taken the required steps to align them with social responsibility and sustainability goals. Reducing ozone-depleting substances, consuming petroleum products, promoting systems powered by recyclable natural resources, and increasing general awareness of environmental issues with societal implications among faculty and students are top priorities for universities today (Hosny et al., 2013).The most frequently used definition of USR focuses on an organization’s capacity for disseminating and utilizing processes in four areas: awareness of social concerns, access to knowledge about social issues, necessary training, and community cooperation (Ali et al., 2021). This categorizes universities according to their capacity to act responsibly in the community (Hopson et al., 2016). ? inquired, ”Is social responsibility a novel model of administrative and academic management in the academic context, or merely a new label for the type of solidarity outreach projects that many universities have pursued for years?”. He emphasized the absence of theoretical definitions that clearly define the scope of CSR. The meaning is still ambiguous and has not been thoroughly examined. Considering the university as a member of society, the USR def- inition can be informed by the CSR conception. Thus, USR definitions vary primarily in the literature, depending on how responsibility is defined and whether the university should be accountable to its students and staff or to stakeholders, partners, and the community (Par- sons, 2014). Carroll (1999) asserts that corporate social responsibility encompasses economic, legal, ethical, and philanthropic responsibilities, implying that firms should function beyond their simply economic and legal tasks. In that regard, higher educational institutions should look beyond their primary missions (student instruction, research development, and commu- nity engagement) and match these missions with USR practice. Reiser (2008) defines USR as Figure 3.1: USR Scope (Ali et al., 2021) labor and environmental impacts produced by the university, in an interactive dialogue with society to promote a sustainable human development.” Nonetheless, Raiser’s definition differs significantly from those proposed by other scholars (Esfijani et al., 2013). According to Mendez (2015), USR promotes an approach to science, technology, and research that values and priori- tizes contributions to the economically disadvantaged.Stewart (2004) also observed that social responsibility concerns in education serve as a foundation for developing appropriate programs that prepare students for various careers while ensuring that underserved groups have access to these programs. The European Commission (2011) asserts that every institution affects society. As such, colleges, like any other institution, must accept responsibility for the effects and consequences of their strategies, structures, policies, and practices (Va ́zquez et al., 2016). The majority of USR definitions originate with academics. USR can be defined as an ad- ministration concept that anticipates universities to consider socially from their fundamental capabilities (Boni and Gasper, 2012). Universities have a social responsibility to contribute to economic, legal, and social growth and achieve social fairness. In this sense, USR fosters genuine multidisciplinary collaboration among educators, scientists, politicians, students, and external stakeholders (e.g., local communities) with the goal of moral edification, education, training, and management (Domanski et al., 2017).USR can be implemented when university leaders highlight public responsibility, ethical behavior, and the importance of practicing good citizenship. University leaders should serve as role models in ethics and promote community health, safety, and environmental protection. Conclusion These synthesis results confirmed that USR initiatives as an excellent tool to attain sustain- ability and enhance university performance worldwide.Although numerous terminologies have been used to define and express the concept of USR in the literature, a university’s social re- sponsibility can be deduced from its partnerships with its stakeholders. A socially responsible university engages with the community through its educational, research, and service-providing functions. abstract: Cette thèse de projet de diplôme d'ingénierie présente les résultats d'un stage de semestre mené chez Devoteam, un cabinet de conseil technologique de premier plan. Le stage a été réalisé en collaboration avec Keep-cool Fitness, un client de Devoteam, avec un accent sur le Machine Learning (ML) et ses applications dans l’analyse de données. L’objectif principal du stage était d’évaluer la qualité des données et les performances de Keep-cool Fitness à travers une analyse initiale de l’indicateur clé de performance (KPI). Sur la base des résultats, le stage visait à proposer des changements à son client. Après cela, nous avons mené une étude d’apprentissage automatique visant à améliorer les pratiques de gestion des données et les processus de prise de décision dans le contexte de l’industrie du gymnase spécifique de Keep-cool Fitness. general_introduction: Machine learning employs algorithms to teach computers to learn from data and make predictions or judgments, hence enabling applications in a wide range of fields. It makes use of statistical models and pattern recognition to extract useful information from large datasets. In recent years, there has been a boom in the use of machine learning and KPIs to solve the issues provided by data complexity and volume. This combination enables firms to get valuable insights, improve performance, and achieve successful outcomes. Devoteam has integrated me into the "Data Driven" department, specifically with the "Data science" team, following the internship application process. This placement involved subcontracting for the company "Keep-cool Fitness" in order to gain a 360- degree view of their customer base. Additionally, it included proposing a machine learning use case to enhance their operations. I began my internship by undergoing comprehensive training, both generic and specialized, to gain access to various projects and commence my work on them. The initial phase involved obtaining certifications, alongside extensive reading of books and scientific literature from diverse domains to acquire a solid understanding of the concept I would be working on. Moreover, I regularly met with my supervisor at the company to ensure ongoing progress and to discuss each task we were actively engaged in. The remainder of the report is organized as follows: The first chapter is about an introduction to Devoteam as long as the project functional requirement, the second chapter is about the literature behind the project, chapter 3 is about our technical decisions for our project, chapter 4 is about the KPI analysis, and finally chapter 5 is about the machine learning analysis
general_conclusion: Finally, my internship with Devoteam Company was extremely gratifying and educational. Throughout the internship, I was able to meet my goals of learning practical industry knowledge and applying my technical talents in a real-world situation. I worked on several important projects, including the creation of a new module that garnered great comments from both clients and the internal team. As a result of my experience, I have gained essential abilities in project management, teamwork, and problem resolution. The difficulties I encountered, such as tight deadlines and limited resources, enabled me to build resilience and adaptation in a fast-paced setting. The usage of key performance indicators (KPIs) and Machine Learning (ML) was critical in monitoring project success and providing significant insights for decision-making. We were able to identify areas for improvement, optimize processes, and ensure project objectives were met as a result of this analysis. I am grateful to my internship supervisor and the entire Devoteam team for their advice, support, and faith in me throughout my internship experience. Their mentoring has greatly aided my personal and professional development. In the long run, this internship has reinforced my interest in the topic and pushed me to pursue higher studies in Machine Learning. My future career path will surely be shaped by the abilities and experiences I gathered throughout this internship
