chapters.Chapter 2 : State of Art: 2.1 Introduction In this chapter, we'll concentrate on the state of the art and talk about the various ideas that have helped us finish our project. We will continually draw attention to the idea of artificial intelligence and how it applies to our endeavor. Finally, we will discuss the various models that were employed as well as the evaluation measurements. 2.2 Data science In the broad subject of data science, knowledge and insights are extracted from data using various statistical and computational methods. It includes several different tasks such data gathering, cleansing, analysis, visualization, and interpretation. Finding patterns in massive datasets that can be used to influence decisions or forecast future events is the aim of data science. With the recent big data explosion, there has been an exponential increase in need for qualified experts that can handle challenging datasets. It is certain that data science will play an increasingly significant role in determining how our world is shaped today and, in the future, as long as organizations continue to rely on data-driven tactics to acquire competitive advantages. 2.3 Artificial intelligence The development of computer systems that are capable of doing activities that traditionally require human intelligence, such as speech recognition, decision-making, and language translation, is known as artificial intelligence (AI). With advancements in deep neural networks and machine learning algorithms, AI has been growing quickly in finance, manufacturing, and transportation. The ethical ramifications of AI development, such as employment displacement and privacy problems, are a concern as well. It will be interesting to see how society adjusts to these changes brought about by artificial intelligence as technology continues to advance at a rapid rate. The lexicons related to AI and most commonly used include:  Machine learning: (ML) is a sub-field of artificial intelligence, it serves as a means to model phenomena, enabling decision-making and addressing challenging or problematic tasks through alternative algorithmic approaches.  Deep learning: (DL) is an automated learning approach that allows for highly abstract modeling of data by using architectures comprising various non-linear formations. In analyses, instead of relying on human processing through pre- labeled algorithms, Deep Learning algorithms directly identify the fundamental treatment characteristics. 2.4 Machine learning A rapidly expanding area of artificial intelligence is machine learning, which entails the creation of algorithms and models that let computers learn from data without being explicitly programmed. It approaches are utilized for projects including fraud detection, recommendation systems, natural language processing, picture identification, and audio recognition. Machine learning has become a crucial tool in extracting insights from enormous datasets that would be impossible for humans alone because of the availability to vast volumes of data generated every day through diverse sources like social media platforms or IoT devices. Machine learning will undoubtedly play a bigger role as we continue to collect more data than ever before thanks to the emergence of big data analytics tools and technological advancements in computer power. Machine learning have 2 sides to it:  Supervised: involves using labeled examples to teach a computer system. These examples, collectively referred to as the training dataset, give the computer context for what is acceptable or unacceptable. The algorithm can predict outcomes for new, unforeseen data by identifying patterns by learning from this labeled data. By giving feedback and revising the algorithm's predictions, a supervisor, usually a human, directs the learning process. The algorithm's accuracy is improved through this iterative process, enabling it to make future The following image shows its exact process: Figure 9: Supervised learning process  Unsupervised: also referred to as unsupervised machine learning, analyzes and groups unlabeled datasets using machine learning algorithms. These algorithms identify hidden patterns or data clusters without the assistance of a human. It is the best option for exploratory data analysis, cross-selling tactics, customer segmentation, and image recognition because of its capacity to find similarities and differences in information. The following image shows its exact schema. Figure 10: Unsupervised learning schema 2.5 Deep learning The very well-known artificial neural networks are used in deep learning, a branch of machine learning, to model and resolve complicated issues. To enable these deep neural networks to learn from patterns and make predictions or judgments without being explicitly programmed, it takes training them on a lot of data. Deep learning has been recognition, image recognition, and natural language processing. It is an effective tool for tackling real-world problems with high accuracy rates because to its capacity for handling unstructured data. Future applications of deep learning are anticipated to become even more as technology continues to advance quickly. The following image shows a deep learning example Neural Network’s scheme Figure 11: Deep learning example schema 2.6 Data mining The practice of extracting patterns, connections, and insightful information from massive data sets is known as data mining. In order to uncover important information that could otherwise remain buried, it includes applying a variety of computational methods and statistical techniques. Organizations can use data mining to find hidden trends, predict the future, and acquire useful information that can inform strategic decision-making. Data mining enables businesses to find patterns, correlations, and anomalies in massive amounts of data, which can reveal important information about consumer behavior, market trends, and operational efficiency. It has applications in many different industries, including business, healthcare, finance, and marketing, and it plays a significant role in extracting important information from complicated datasets. The following image shows the steps of normal data mining process. Figure 12: Data mining steps 2.7 Method of comparative filtering: Data can be filtered and prioritized using the comparative filtering method in data science by comparing various attributes or criteria. To determine their relevance or significance, data points or variables are compared to a list of predetermined criteria or thresholds. Data scientists can pinpoint and concentrate on particular subsets of data that meet particular requirements or exhibit desired characteristics by using comparative filtering. This technique facilitates effective decision-making and the extraction of insights by condensing the data to a more manageable and significant subset. 2.8 Categorical data Categorical data, also referred to as qualitative data, is a type of information that is identified and categorized using names, labels, or specific categories. Categorical data, as opposed to numerical data, which can be measured on a continuous scale, represents discrete variables that can be arranged into distinct groups or classes. Each data point can only belong to one of these categories if they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Frequently, characteristics, attributes, or qualities such as gender, marital status, product types, or customer preferences that cannot be expressed solely through numerical values are represented by categorical data. As the emphasis is on understanding the distribution, frequencies, and relationships between categories, categorical data analysis requires different statistical techniques and visualization methods than does numerical data analysis. The following image shows different types of data, including categorical data. Figure 13: Different data types 2.9 Key Performance Indicator KPIs, also known as key success indicators (KSIs), differ between businesses and industries based on performance standards. A software company, for instance, might use year-over-year (YOY) revenue growth as its main performance indicator in order to achieve the fastest growth in its sector. A retail chain, on the other hand, might value same-store sales as the best KPI metric for assessing growth. Data collection, storage, cleaning, and synthesizing are the foundation of KPIs. The data could pertain to any division across the entire company and could be either financial or non-financial in nature. KPIs' objective is to clearly communicate results so that management can make more informed strategic decisions. 2.10 Model used in our study 2.10.1 Clustering As part of the clustering data analysis technique, similar data points are grouped together based on common traits or patterns. It is a method of unsupervised learning that seeks to identify the underlying structure in a dataset. In order to quantify the similarity between data points, clustering mathematically entails defining a similarity or distance metric. The Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance, or cosine similarity are examples of commonly used distance metrics. Let's use the Euclidean distance as an illustration. Given two data points x and y, each represented as d-dimensional vectors (x1, x2, , x_d) and (y1, y2, , y_d), the Euclidean distance between them is calculated as: This equation calculates the d-dimensional space's shortest straight-line distance between any two points. The Euclidean distance is used to measure how similar two data points are. Several algorithms, including K-means, hierarchical clustering, and DBSCAN (Density- Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise), can be used to perform clustering. Based on similarity metrics, these algorithms assign data points to clusters using various mathematical techniques. According to (Farley and Raftery, 1998), clustering composes of 2 parts:  Hierarchical Methods: Agglomerative, Divisive Hierarchical, etc.  Partitioning Methods: K-Means etc. 2.10.1.1 Partitioning methods Partitional clustering, also known as partitioning clustering, is a clustering technique used to divide observations contained within a data set into various groups according to how similar they are. The analyst must specify the desired number of clusters when using the algorithms. 2.10.1.1.1 K_Means The K-means algorithm is an iterative clustering technique that aims to partition a dataset into K distinct clusters. The algorithm follows these steps:  Randomly initialize K cluster centroids. Each centroid represents the center of a cluster.  Assign each data point to the nearest centroid based on the Euclidean distance. The distance between a data point x and a centroid μ is calculated using the formula: d(x, μ) = sqrt((x1 - μ1)2 + (x2 - μ2)2 + + (x_d - μ_d)2) Here, (x1, x2, , x_d) represents the coordinates of the data point x, and (μ1, μ2, , μ_d) represents the coordinates of the centroid μ.  Recalculate the centroids by taking the mean of all the data points assigned to each cluster. The new centroid position is computed using the formula: μ = (1 / n) * Σi xi, with n represents the number of data points assigned to the cluster.  Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the cluster assignments no longer change significantly or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The objective of the K-means algorithm is to minimize the within-cluster sum of squared distances, known as the distortion or inertia. The distortion is calculated using the formula: J = Σj Σi ||xi - μ_j||2 With xi equals a data point, μ_j denotes the centroid of the j-th cluster, and ||xi - μ_j|| represents the Euclidean distance between the data point and the centroid. The K-means algorithm ensures that the data points within each cluster are near their respective centroid and that the clusters are well-separated by minimizing the distortion. When it comes to tasks like customer segmentation, image compression, or anomaly detection, K-means clustering is frequently used because it allows for the analysis and decision-making process to focus on similar data points. Figure 14: A K-Means visualization example 2.10.1.1.2 K_Means ++ It is similar to the algorithm of clustering K-Means but improves the centroid initialization step by considering the distance between data points when selecting the initial centroids.  It selects the first centroid randomly from the dataset.  For each subsequent centroid, calculate the distance (using Euclidean distance) between each data point and the nearest centroid already selected.  Then chooses the next centroid from the remaining data points with a probability proportional to the squared distance to its nearest centroid. This ensures that the new centroid is far from the existing ones.  Then finally it repeats steps b and c until K centroids are selected. 2.10.1.1.3 Unsupervised K-Means: It is also a derivative of K-Means clustering algorithm but the difference between the normal one and the unsupervised one is that it automatically determines the optimal number of clusters. Here are the steps of U-K-means algorithm. First it specifies a range of potential cluster numbers, we should define a minimum value for the number of clusters (K_min) and a maximum value (K_max) that you want to consider. Then, for each K value in the range [K_min, K_max]:  It applies the K-means algorithm with the current K value to the dataset.  It calculates an evaluation criterion, such as the elbow method or silhouette score, to assess the quality of the clustering for the current K value.  Then, stores the evaluation criterion value for the current K. After that it proceeds to determine the optimal number of clusters:  Analyze the evaluation criterion values obtained for different K values.  Pick the K-value that makes the evaluation criterion its maximum. For the elbow method, locate the "elbow" point in the plot where more clusters are added but the criterion is not significantly improved. As an alternative, select the K value with the silhouette score that maximizes the average silhouette coefficient. Finally, it applies the K-means algorithm with the optimal number of clusters:  Use the optimal K value that was found.  Use the dataset with the chosen K value to run the K-means algorithm.  Obtain the clustering's final results. 2.10.1.2 Hierarchical Methods When using a hierarchical clustering technique, data objects are combined to form a tree of clusters. Top-down or bottom-up algorithms are used in hierarchical clustering. Due to its inability to implement adjustment after a merge or split decision has been made, an authentic hierarchical clustering method loses quality. 2.10.1.2.1 Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering AHC is a bottom-up clustering technique in which sub-clusters of clusters have sub- clusters of their own, etc. Each object is first located in its cluster, and then these atomic clusters are combined to form larger and larger clusters until all the objects are in one cluster, or until a certain termination condition is met. The majority of hierarchical clustering techniques are used for this category. They differ solely in how they define similarity between clusters. 2.10.2 Association Rule Mining The potent method association rule mining can uncover hidden relationships and connections between variables in large datasets. It is frequently used in data mining and machine learning and has a variety of uses, including fraud detection, market basket analysis, and client segmentation. Association rule mining helps companies better understand client behavior, improve marketing plans, and spot anomalies or suspicious activity by detecting patterns and correlations between variables. It is a useful tool for decision-making and enhancing operational efficiency in many sectors due to its capacity to reveal hidden relationships. Figure 15: Association rules concept The image describe the concept of Association Rule Mining(ARM) “Associating things/objects by using some rules.” 2.10.2.1 Apriori The "beer and diaper" tale is the most well-known association rule mining tale. Customers who purchase diapers also frequently purchase alcohol, according to research. This well- known illustration demonstrates the possibility of numerous intriguing association rules being concealed in our daily data. Association rule mining is a method for figuring out the underlying connections between various things. There are numerous ways to carry out association rule mining. The easiest and most direct method is the Apriori algorithm, which we will discuss in this post. However, because it's the fundamental approach, a variety of enhancements can be made to it. First, it initializes the process by scanning the dataset to identify the support count of each individual item. The support count represents the number of transactions in which an item appears. Secondly, it generates frequent item sets of size 1 (single items) by selecting items that meet a minimum support threshold set by the user. Then, while there are frequent item sets of size k (k > 1), continue the following steps:  Generates candidate item sets of size k+1 by joining pairs of frequent item sets of size k.  Prunes the candidate item sets by removing those that have subsets of size k that are not frequent.  Scan the dataset again to count the support of each candidate itemset and determine which ones meet the minimum support threshold. The process then goes back to Step 3 and continues it until no more frequent item sets can be produced. Moreover, it extracts association rules from the frequent item sets. An association rule consists of an antecedent (a set of items) and a consequent (a single item). The rules are generated by splitting each frequent itemset into all possible non-empty subsets and forming rules with the remaining items as the consequent. Finally, it extracts association rules from the frequent item sets. An association rule consists of an antecedent (a set of items) and a consequent (a single item). The rules are generated by splitting each frequent itemset into all possible non-empty subsets and forming rules with the remaining items as the consequent. 2.11 Validity measures In data analysis, validity measures evaluate the reliability and accuracy of the conclusions drawn from a given approach or model. These metrics aid in assessing how accurately the data analysis method catches the desired information or accurately depicts the underlying reality. Metrics like precision, recall, accuracy, F1 score, or correlation coefficients are examples of validity measures. Researchers and practitioners can have confidence in the accuracy and value of their findings by assessing the validity of the analysis, ensuring that the inferences made from the data are accurate and reliable. 2.11.1 Silhouette Coefficient The quality of clustering findings is measured using the silhouette score. In comparison to nearby clusters, it assesses how well each data point fits into the one to which it has been assigned. A higher silhouette score means that the data point is properly clustered, whilst a lower value implies that it might be misclassified. Each sample's Silhouette Coefficient is defined, and it consists of two scores:  The mean distance between a sample and all other points in the same class.  The mean distance between a sample and all other points in the next nearest cluster. The image below shows the Silhouette Coefficient s for a single sample. 2.11.2 Calinski-Harabasz Index To assess the caliber of clustering results, one can utilize the Calinski-Harabasz index. By taking into account both the within-cluster and between-cluster dispersion, it measures the distance between clusters. Better-defined and more distinct clusters are indicated by a higher Calinski-Harabasz index, whereas less separation between clusters is suggested by a lower index. This method main advantages:  The score is higher when clusters are dense and well separated, which relates to a standard concept of a cluster.  The score is fast to compute. 2.11.3 Davies-Bouldin Index This index represents the average "similarity"—a metric that contrasts the size of the clusters with the distance between them—between clusters. The lowest possible score is zero. Values that are nearer to 0 denote better partitions. Its advantages:  The computation of Davies-Bouldin is simpler than that of Silhouette scores.  The index is solely based on quantities and features inherent to the dataset as its computation only uses point-wise distances. Its drawbacks:  The Davies-Boulding index is generally higher for convex clusters than other concepts of clusters, such as density-based clusters like those obtained from DBSCAN.  The usage of centroid distance limits the distance metric to Euclidean space. chapters.Chapter 5 : Business Value: 5.1 Introduction In this chapter, we will see the model selection, pre-processing phase, as well as, Data mining processes, with all its parts (pre-knowledge methods, models, evaluation). By the end of this chapter, we will discuss different conclusion that we had come up based on our preferred method. 5.2 Model selection So, we are dealing with unsupervised learning, we have our data without any corresponding target variables. In this case we are dealing clustering and association rules primarily. However, clustering has a lot of sub types, and a lot of those subtypes cannot work for us perhaps. If we look on the type of our data, in our case, we do have mainly categorical data, and according to this (Oyelade, Jelili, 2019), best clustering algorithm for us is partitional, hierarchical, soft clustering method, as well as some model-based methods. For us we are going to pick K mean clustering as our partitional method, and agglomerative clustering as our hierarchical method. As for picking algorithm based on the size of our data, we don’t have to worry about, because we only deal with 545 rows and 41 columns after preprocessing as we going to see. 5.3 Pre-processing 5.3.1 Feature selections Based on domain knowledge, we have selected 5 variables, that are going to really describe our client’s behaviors that we want to study, those variables are: “Your age” “How important is exercise to you ?” “How do you describe your current level of fitness ?” “How often do you exercise?” “What barriers, if any, prevent you from exercising more regularly? (Please select all that apply)” Figure 65: Head of our data frame after feature selection Eliminating by that variables that are so obvious far away from our purpose such as: “Your gender” “Would you say you eat a healthy balanced diet ?” “What prevent you from eating a healthy balanced diet” Table 6: Example of columns filtered in feature selection stage 5.3.2 Encoding categorical variables 5.3.2.1 Problem encountered: more than one instance in the cell Before encoding our variables notice we have more than one instance in one cell for “What barriers, if any, prevent you from exercising more regularly? (Please select all that apply)” column that we did rename it into: “exercise barriers” Figure 66: “exercise barriers” before data cleaning We did eventually resolve the problem by creating Barriers1, Barriers2, , BarriersN columns such as N is the number of maximum number of semicolons in one cell. Then we precede giving each column with the instances that it has. The figure below shows our resulted dataset. Figure 67: “exercise barriers” after treatments. Now, if we will be working with categorical variables doing some clustering it is essential to encode our variables since most if not all clustering algorithms don’t take strings for inputs. We did have primarily this dataset below. Figure 68: Head of data frame after “exercise barriers” treatments 5.3.2.2 Encoding categorical variables Then after encoding with dummy encoding additionally to some normal processing the resulted dataset is shown in the figure below. Figure 69: Head of data frame after dummy encoding 5.3.3 Encoding the numerical variable In this step, we’ve transformed the column “exercise importancy” with is non the less that “How important is exercise to you ?” from this: Figure 70: “exercise importancy” before treatment. Into a column with the maximum is 1 and the minimum is 0 to be similar to our other columns that we have encoded previously. The new “exercise importancy” is shown in the figure below. Figure 71: “exercise importancy” after treatment. Resulting in our well processed data set that we will be working with in the next phase which is the modeling phase. Figure 72: Head of data frame after data pre-processing 5.4 Data mining process 5.4.1 Pre- knowledge methods 5.4.1.1 The elbow method We have iterated over a range of numbers of clusters, calculated their within cluster of squares (WCSS), then we’ve plotted the results against the number of clusters to visualize. Here is the result visualization below. Figure 73: Elbow method As we can see, there is no obvious reduction of the rate of the WCSS where the (elbow) is shown. Therefore, we haven’t stopped right at this method. 5.4.1.2 The silhouette score method We have now iterated over numbers of clusters using the K Means, same as before, we have then plotted the silhouette scores against the number of clusters in order to identify the number that maximize the overall cohesion and separation of the data points within clusters like shown in the figure below. Figure 74: Silhouette score method According to the silhouette score, we have, within the range of 1 to 10, 4 good cluster number. That’s why we should conduct another study to see 5.4.1.3 Gap statistic method We have generated multiple random reference datasets and applies the K-means clustering algorithm to each reference dataset for different numbers of clusters within the specified range. The within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) is calculated for each clustering result, and then displayed in the graph below. 5.4.2 Models 5.4.2.1 Partitional clustering 5.4.2.1.1 Unsupervised-K-Means We still have some doubt for the number of clusters to use, thus we thought we could use another method that according to this paper (Sinaga, Kristina P and Miin-Shen Yang, 2020), we could generate a clustering model without even inputting a number of clusters. And so, we could utilize the U-K-Means like a forth pre-knowledge method to support our 3 previous methods, and also like a clustering method. Figure 76: U-K-Mean clustering The figure above shows visualization of the U-K-Means using the PCA method. We can clearly see that 4 is the optimal number of clusters according to the U-K-Means. 5.4.2.1.2 K-Means Using also the PCA method, the figure below is a visualization of K-Means algorithm using 4 clusters. Figure 77: K-Mean clustering The evaluation of the method is in the sections to come. 5.4.2.1.3 K-Means ++ If we want to augment both the speed and the accuracy of the K-Means algorithm we need use the another version of the k-means, at least according to (Arthur David, and Sergei Vassilvitskii, 2007) The figure below shows the visualization of the K-Means++. 5.4.2.2 Hierarchal clustering 5.4.2.2.1 Agglomerative clustering How about clustering in another way that isn’t partitioning? Well, we need to look at hierarchical clustering, and see how agglomerative will work with us. This figure is about the dendrogram; it displays how individual data points or clusters are merged together at each step of the clustering process. Figure 79: Dendrogram of Hierarchical Clustering And the figure below is a normal PCA representation in a 2 dimensional space. Figure 80: Agglomerative clustering We have chosen to work with ward distance to have a compactness and well separation of clusters plus good scalability according to a paper of (Murtagh, Fionn,, Pedro Contreras, 2012) 5.4.3 Evaluations The table below shows the 3 metrics of evaluation that we are going to use to put our clustering models into evaluation. Clustering U-K-Means K-Means K- Agglomerative algorithm Means++ Calinski 58.85 55.83 58.85 213.71 Harabasz Index (CHI) Silhouette 0.13 0.12 0.13 0.25 Index (SWI) Davies 2.21 2.36 2.21 1.52 Bouldin Index (BDI) Table 7: Evaluation table of our models According to this table, we will consider that Agglomerative clustering is the best model in our situation. Since it has the biggest CHI, the closest SWI to 1, and the smallest BDI compared to other methods. 5.5 Interpretation Now we are going to interpret the Agglomerative clustering results by analyzing the resulting clusters and understanding the relationship between data points within each cluster. We’ve assigned cluster labels to each data point. The cluster labels indicate which cluster a data point belongs to. And based on this, we have generated a code that assigns cluster labels to each data point. The cluster labels indicate which cluster a data point belongs to. Here are the results.  Cluster 1: Dominant Age Fitness level Barriers Exercise Groups impotency 19-25 Good No barriers 0<0.80<1 15-18 Table 8: Cluster 1 This cluster represents the group of people the fit people that love to exercise  Cluster 2: Dominant Age Fitness level Barriers Exercise Groups impotency 19-25 Average Lacking 0<0.67<1 15-18 Unfit motivation +Tiredness Table 9: Cluster 2 This cluster represents those who are the most unfit in all our groups.  Cluster 3: Dominant Age Fitness level Barriers Exercise Groups impotency 19-25 Average Tiredness 0<0.62<1 15-18 Table 10: Cluster 3 This group is the one with the lowest exercise impotency.  Cluster 4: Dominant Age Fitness level Barriers Exercise Groups impotency 19-25 Average Lacking 0<0.68<1 15-18 Good motivation Table 11: Cluster 4 If we took at the results we can see that our 4 groups divided by their fit level accordingly: cluster 1 than 4, after that we have cluster 3 and finally with the lowest fitness level is cluster 2. Those groups have different barriers, if we focus on solving cluster 2,3 and 4’s barriers we could obtain a group of people that love sports theoretically. However, if we examined the barriers of each of those groups we can clearly conclude that if we prioritize solving the ussie of tiredness in group cluster 2, theoretically we can transform it into group cluster 4 with exercise impotency 0.68. And it is already a win. 5.6 Conclusion In summary, this chapter has shown how machine learning models may be used to recognize clusters and extract important data from large datasets. The research advances the science of machine learning and has potential for real-world applications across a range of sectors. Clustering methods will continue to be improved by more study in this field, which will ultimately increase their usefulness in practical situations. Conclusion Finally, my internship with Devoteam Company was extremely gratifying and educational. Throughout the internship, I was able to meet my goals of learning practical industry knowledge and applying my technical talents in a real-world situation. I worked on several important projects, including the creation of a new module that garnered great comments from both clients and the internal team. As a result of my experience, I have gained essential abilities in project management, teamwork, and problem resolution. The difficulties I encountered, such as tight deadlines and limited resources, enabled me to build resilience and adaptation in a fast-paced setting. The usage of key performance indicators (KPIs) and Machine Learning (ML) was critical in monitoring project success and providing significant insights for decision-making. We were able to identify areas for improvement, optimize processes, and ensure project objectives were met as a result of this analysis. I am grateful to my internship supervisor and the entire Devoteam team for their advice, support, and faith in me throughout my internship experience. Their mentoring has greatly aided my personal and professional development. In the long run, this internship has reinforced my interest in the topic and pushed me to pursue higher studies in Machine Learning. titre: TRINO INTEGRATION WITH ORACLE INTELLIGENT DATA LAKE
author: ISMAIL CHENTOUF
abstract: Dans le cadre de mon stage au sein d’Oracle Labs Morocco, intégré à l’équipe Analytics – Big Data Service (BDS), j’ai joué un rôle clé dans l’amélioration des capacités de Trino en tant que moteur SQL distribué haute performance, dédié à l’analyse de données à grande échelle. Mon principal objectif était d’optimiser l’intégration de Trino avec Oracle Intelligent Data Lake, en assurant une interopérabilité fluide avec Hadoop, Hive et d’autres technologies big data de l’écosystème cloud d’Oracle. L’une de mes contributions majeures a été l’amélioration du TrinoWrapper, un composant middleware essentiel permettant à Trino de comprendre et d’interagir avec l’infrastructure de données d’Oracle. J’ai dirigé la mise à niveau de TrinoWrapper pour qu’il soit compatible avec la dernière version de Trino, en y intégrant de nouvelles fonctionnalités tout en garantissant la rétrocompatibilité et des performances élevées. J’ai également optimisé la connectivité avec le metastore, notamment Hive, afin de réduire la latence des requêtes et d’améliorer l’efficacité de la récupération des métadonnées. Pour accélérer les performances des requêtes, j’ai perfectionné l’interaction de Trino avec la couche de stockage, permettant un accès plus rapide aux données dans le cadre de traitements analytiques complexes. Sur le plan de l’infrastructure, j’ai utilisé Java, Python, Docker et Kubernetes (OKE – Oracle Kubernetes Engine) pour automatiser les déploiements, résoudre les problèmes de cluster et gérer Trino dans des environnements cloud. Mon travail a contribué directement à la mission d’Oracle, qui est de fournir une plateforme de données robuste, évolutive et performante, en combinant la rapidité d’exécution de Trino avec la sécurité et la fiabilité de niveau entreprise offertes par BDS. Cette expérience a enrichi mes compétences en développement Java, systèmes distribués, optimisation de requêtes et architectures cloud-native, tout en soulignant l’importance de la collaboration interdisciplinaire dans le développement de solutions big data de pointe. Mots clés : BDS, OCI, Trino, OKE, Java, Python, Shell, Ambari, Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD

general_introduction: This report presents the outcome of my internship experience at Oracle Labs Morocco within the Analytics – Big Data Services (BDS) division. It is structured to guide the reader through both the organizational context and the technical work carried out during the internship. We will start by introducing Oracle as a global technology leader, detailing its products, services, and organizational structure. This section will provide a foundational understanding of the company’s mission and its positioning in the enterprise technology landscape. Following that, the report will present a comprehensive overview of Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC), its main features, and the value it offers to enterprise customers. We will also introduce Oracle’s Big Data Service (BDS), highlighting its technical architecture, use cases, and the business problems it addresses. The next part of the report will focus on the methodologies and tools used throughout the internship. We will describe the hybrid Agile approach adopted by the team, as well as the collaborative ecosystem built around tools such as Slack, Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket, which supported our day-to-day work and communication. After setting this context, we will move on to the core of the report: a detailed technical study. This includes the analysis of an existing problem related to Trino’s integration with the Oracle Intelligent Data Lake (OIDL), the challenges caused by tight dependencies, and the proposed architecture to decouple and optimize the integration. We will explain the solution implemented, including the development of a custom Trino wrapper, the OCI Metastore plugin, and an upgrade of Trino from version 389 to 468. This part also includes our learnings from working with Kubernetes (OKE) and the Trino Operator. Finally, the report concludes with a general conclusion summarizing the results of the internship, the technical and personal growth achieved, and the future work that could continue building on what was developed
general_conclusion: This report reflects the contributions and progress achieved during my internship at Oracle Labs Morocco, where I worked as part of the Analytics Big-Data-Service (BDS) team. The internship centered around improving the integration of Trino, a distributed SQL query engine, with Oracle’s Intelligent Data Lake, a key component in Oracle’s cloud-native big data platform. Throughout this experience, I tackled challenges related to large-scale distributed systems, focusing on optimizing the TrinoWrapper, ensuring compatibility with the latest Trino release, and enhancing metastore interactions with Hive. These improvements helped reduce query latency and increased metadata retrieval efficiency, contributing within Oracle’s cloud ecosystem. Beyond the technical aspects, this internship offered a valuable opportunity to collaborate with experienced engineers across various teams and regions, which helped me grow both professionally and personally. It deepened my understanding of distributed systems, query performance tuning, and cloud-native development practices. Overall, I am proud of the work accomplished during this internship and excited about the remaining opportunities to contribute. This experience has been both enriching and formative, setting a strong foundation for future work in cloud-based data systems and large-scale analytics solutions

Oracle Oracle Corporation is an American multinational computer technology company headquartered in Austin, Texas. Co-founded in 1977 in Santa Clara, California, by Larry Ellison, who remains executive chairman, Oracle was the third-largest software company in the world in 2020 by revenue and market capitalization. The company's 2023 ranking in the Forbes Global 2000 was 80 [1]. Figure 1 -Oracle Headquarters Redwood Shores. A pioneer in database software, Oracle is best known for its relational database management systems (RDBMS), in which it remains the global market leader. The company also specializes in cloud infrastructure (Oracle Cloud), enterprise resource planning (ERP), customer relationship management (CRM), and supply chain management (SCM) solutions. Oracle Labs : Oracle Labs is the company's research and development section, and it focuses on developing technologies that will maintain Oracle at the forefront of the IT industry. tasks or projects that would be difficult to execute within a product development organization due to high risk or uncertainty. Oracle Labs research is focused on real-world applications, and the researchers are aiming to develop technologies that will have a significant impact on how society and technology progress. Introduction to Big Data Service (BDS) Oracle Big Data Service (BDS) is a fully managed cloud platform designed to process, store, and analyze large-scale structured and unstructured data. It provides an integrated environment for big data technologies such as Hadoop, Spark, Kafka, and Hive, enabling enterprises to build scalable data lakes, perform real-time analytics, and run machine learning workloads. Figure 11 - OCI Big Data with Apache Hadoop [9]. 🔹 Data Sources On the left side, we see data ingestion sources from: • On-premises systems, such as Hadoop clusters and Oracle Big Data Appliances. • Cloud-based platforms, including Cloudera, AWS EMR, Azure HDInsight, and Databricks. This showcases Oracle BDS’s flexibility and compatibility with existing big data ecosystems, enabling seamless migration or hybrid architecture. 🔹 Core of Oracle Big Data Service At the center is OCI Big Data, which serves as the main processing environment. It integrates with a wide range of Apache and open-source technologies, including: • Apache Spark: For in-memory distributed data processing. • Apache Hive, HBase, Ranger, and Oozie: For querying, storage, security, and workflow orchestration. • Kafka: For real-time data streaming. • Delta Lake and Parquet: For data storage formats supporting ACID transactions and efficient analytics. • JupyterHub: For interactive data exploration and notebooks. • Trino (formerly Presto): For distributed SQL querying across different sources. • Other tools like Sqoop, Ambari, Zookeeper, and Hue provide additional functionality in administration, data movement, and visualization. This extensive toolset allows enterprises to build customizable big data pipelines suited for batch, real-time, and advanced analytics use cases. 🔹 Integrated OCI Services At the bottom, the diagram highlights OCI-native services that enhance Oracle BDS: • OCI Data Lake: Unified storage for structured and unstructured data. • OCI Data Catalog: Metadata management and data governance. • OCI Data Flow: Serverless Spark processing for simplified ETL and ML pipelines. • OCI Data Science: For training and deploying machine learning models at scale. 1.1. Technical Architecture & Key Component Cluster Structure Oracle Big Data Service (BDS) utilizes a multi-node cluster architecture designed to ensure high performance, scalability, and fault tolerance. The Master Nodes are responsible for managing cluster coordination and metadata through services like HDFS NameNode and YARN ResourceManager, while also hosting critical components such as the Hive Metastore and Spark History Server in a high-availability (HA) configuration to eliminate single points of failure. Worker Nodes handle the execution of data processing workloads using engines like Spark and MapReduce, and store data across HDFS DataNodes, allowing for horizontal scaling to accommodate growing data volumes. Utility Nodes provide edge services , and act as gateways for client connections, enabling user interaction with the cluster. Figure 12 - OCI Big Data service cluster Architecture Core Software Stack: The Oracle Big Data Service (BDS) leverages a curated stack of robust, open-source technologies to provide a powerful and flexible platform for big data processing and analytics. Key components include: Apache Hadoop in BDS: At the core of Oracle Big Data Service (BDS) is Apache Hadoop, which provides essential distributed storage and resource management for large-scale data processing. HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System): Core storage system, distributing data across Worker Nodes with replication. Master Nodes (NameNode) manage metadata; Worker Nodes (DataNodes) store data blocks. YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator): Handles cluster resources. The ResourceManager (Master) allocates resources globally; NodeManagers (Workers) manage local execution. Supports multiple engines like Spark and MapReduce. Apache Spark in BDS: Apache Spark is a high-speed, general-purpose cluster computing engine used in BDS for a wide variety of data processing tasks. High-Performance Computing: Uses RDDs, DataFrames, and MLlib for batch, SQL, streaming, and graph analytics. YARN Integration: Spark runs on YARN — the driver requests resources from the ResourceManager, and executors run in containers on Worker Nodes. Apache Hive in BDS: Apache Hive provides a SQL-like interface for querying and analyzing large datasets stored in distributed environments such as HDFS. SQL-Based Data Warehousing: Hive enables data analysts to run SQL-like queries (HiveQL) on massive datasets stored in HDFS. These queries are internally converted into jobs (MapReduce, Tez, or Spark), making big data processing accessible to users without deep programming knowledge. Hive Metastore (HMS): schemas, data locations, and partitions. Hosted on Master Nodes and backed by a relational database, HMS allows various engines (like Hive, Spark, Trino) to access consistent data definitions, ensuring seamless interoperability and unified data access across the BDS ecosystem. Component Role in BDS HDFS Distributed storage for batch data Resource management for YARN Spark/MapReduce SQL-based querying & metadata Hive management Spark Fast in-memory processing (ETL, ML) Federated SQL queries across multiple Trino sources Data Storage and Management : Effective data storage and management are essential for any big data platform. Oracle BDS offers reliable solutions for both active, high-performance processing and persistent, low-cost storage. Primary Storage (HDFS on local disks of Worker Nodes) : BDS uses Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) as its main storage layer, deployed across local disks of Worker Nodes. Each node runs a DataNode that manages physical storage of data blocks. This co-location of compute and storage ensures data locality, minimizing network transfer and maximizing throughput for Spark and MapReduce jobs. HDFS provides fault tolerance by replicating data blocks across nodes. However, this storage is tied to the cluster’s lifecycle and hardware limits. Integration with OCI Object Storage : OCI Object Storage complements HDFS by offering highly durable and scalable cloud-based storage that persists beyond the life of a BDS cluster. Persistent and Cost-Effective Storage : Unlike HDFS, OCI Object Storage retains data even when clusters are shut down. Its scalable and economical pricing makes it ideal for long-term data lakes, archiving, and staging areas. Backup and Disaster Recovery : BDS can back up HDFS data and metadata to Object Storage, creating a reliable disaster recovery option. Data Source and Sink : With native connectors, BDS applications can read from and write to OCI Object Storage, enabling use cases like data ingestion, results export, and data sharing across platforms. Decoupling Compute and Storage: This integration allows compute and storage to operate independently—BDS clusters can be started and stopped on demand, while Object Storage safely retains the data, improving cost efficiency and flexibility. Security : Oracle BDS implements a multi-layered security framework to protect data and infrastructure. The service enforces Kerberos authentication for robust cluster access control, ensuring only authorized users and services can interact with the Hadoop ecosystem. All data transfers are secured through TLS encryption, while sensitive keys are managed and rotated automatically using OCI Vault for enhanced protection. Network isolation is achieved through Virtual Cloud Network (VCN) segmentation, preventing unauthorized external access. Additionally, granular IAM policies enable role-based access control (RBAC), allowing administrators to define precise permissions for users and applications accessing BDS resources. Together, these measures provide end-to-end security—from authentication to data protection— while maintaining compliance with enterprise security standards. Figure 13 - OCI Big Data service security 1.2. chapters.Chapter 3: Technical Study: 1. Introduction After analyzing our project, it is essential to take a closer look at its technical aspects. It also discusses the programming languages and tools used throughout the project. 2. Problem analysis and Solution Proposal 2.1. Oracle Intelligent Data Lake (OIDL) VS Oracle Big Data Service (BDS) : Oracle Intelegent Data Lake: Oracle Intelligent Data Lake, a key enabler of the Oracle Data Intelligence Platform The new Oracle Intelligent Data Lake will rearchitect services such as OCI Data Lake, OCI Data Catalog, OCI Data Integration, OCI Data Flow with Apache Spark, and Jupyter Notebook capabilities into a single cohesive environment for building data lakes, extending analytical applications with real-time data, transforming data, and creating end-to-end data orchestration. [16] Oracle’s Data Intelligence vision is unique, because it includes content, in the form of Data Intelligence apps, and capabilities, in the form of a unified Data Intelligence Platform. No other cloud hyperscaler or specialist provider can match the span of value and vision offered by this combination. -key advantages for data initiatives: BDS provides a configurable Hadoop/Spark platform but requires organizations to manually integrate and manage data ingestion, cataloging, governance, and analytics—demanding specialized skills and effort. OIDL simplifies this with a fully managed, pre-integrated environment, combining: • Data lake storage (OCI Object Storage) • Data integration (OCI Data Integration) • Cataloging (OCI Data Catalog) • Spark processing (OCI Data Flow) • Notebooks (Jupyter) Key benefits: Reduced operational overhead Oracle handles patching, maintenance, and interoperability. Faster time-to-value Pre-built integrations accelerate pipeline development Simplified governance Unified control plane and shared metadata streamline management Lower skill barrier More accessible to non-experts compared to managing standalone components. Focus on insights Teams spend less time on infrastructure and more on analytics. Better collaboration Shared environment for engineers, scientists, and analysts. While BDS offers strong foundational capabilities, OIDL delivers a more efficient, user-friendly solution for modern data lakes and analytics. 2.2 Understanding the problem Deumciption: Oracle's new Intelligent Data Lake (IDL) aims to provide a cohesive, fully managed environment by integrating services like OCI Data Lake, Data Catalog, and Data Integration, with Apache Spark as a key runtime. While this unified approach simplifies data operations, its fully managed nature means users currently have a curated set of tools, primarily centered around Spark. This contrasts with more flexible platforms like Oracle Big Data Service (BDS), where users can customize their environment by adding or removing components like Spark or Trino. The specific problem being addressed is that IDL, in its current iteration, does not offer Trino as an alternative or complementary runtime, potentially limiting users from leveraging Trino's superior performance for interactive, ad-hoc SQL queries where it often outpaces Spark, thus not fully optimizing the analytical capabilities of the "intelligent" data lake for all query types. 2.3 Solution Trino Integration with Oracle Intelligent Data Lake Our proposed solution is to implement Trino as , high-performance distributed SQL query engine. This strategy effectively decouples our query processing (compute) from our data storage. For the deployment, we will leverage Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) to orchestrate the Trino cluster, deploying the official container images for its coordinator and worker nodes. This approach provides a scalable and resilient foundation, allowing us to manage the runtime efficiently. The most critical integration step will be to configure Trino's Hive catalog to connect to our existing Hive Metastore (HMS) endpoint. By doing this, we grant Trino immediate access to the metadata for all our tables—including their schemas and data locations—enabling analysts to run fast, interactive queries across our data lake without requiring any data migration. By containerizing these instances, BDS can easily deploy and manage them. This means that whether you’re running analytics on a developer's laptop or in a production environment, everything works the same way. ▪ Multi-Tenant Architecture: In a multi-tenant setup, multiple customers (tenants) share the same infrastructure. Docker helps by isolating each tenant’s services and instances in separate ▪ Scalability: One of the great things about Docker is that it makes scaling applications up or down very straightforward. This flexibility ensures that BDS can handle varying workloads efficiently. ▪ Consistent Deployment: Docker ensures that software runs the same way, no matter where it’s deployed. This consistency reduces issues when moving software from development to production, making deployments smoother and more predictable. ▪ Better Resource Use: Docker allows multiple containers to run on the same host machine, which means better utilization of resources. This efficiency is important for managing costs and ensuring optimal performance. As such, by integrating Docker, BDS is capable of presenting credible and dependable analytics services that can scale up as well as do more in a shorter time frame. Thus, since microservices and analytic instances can be containerized, it is easier to maintain and adjust intricate systems to guarantee that BDS effectively fulfills users’ demands. 2.2.10. Kubernetes Figure 32 - Kubernetes Logo Kubernetes is an open source technology that is used for operations of planning, deployment, management, and scaling of software applications that are shipped in a container. Currently. The brains of the Kubernetes structure are embedded into the new architecture. ▪ Container Orchestration: Kubernetes is used to automate the process of running Docker container and managing it . It oversees where containers are placed on different machines, oversees loads, and checks whether the application is in order or not. ▪ Efficient Resource Use: This way Kubernetes helps to manage the resources properly as resources are properly aligned with the containers. It can also prioritize users more efficiently and assign them resources based on utilization, normally called customer, hence they will only get the amount they want, sparing time and money. ▪ Scalability: Kubernetes makes it easy to scale applications up or down. If there’s an increase in demand, Kubernetes can quickly spin up additional containers. When demand decreases, it scales back to save resources. This automatic scaling ensures that applications can handle varying loads without manual intervention. ▪ High Availability: Kubernetes actively tracks the wellness of containers and can automatically recover or self-remediate gone awry as well as the containers. This selfhealing indicates that the applications being offered would be available and have the capacity to bounce back in case of a failure as they are customer-oriented. ▪ Load Balancing: This is an advantage because Kubernetes has the ability to split traffic evenly across the containers, so one container does not get more load than the other is meant to take. This load balancing brings about the achievement of balance in the performance and the avoidance of potential slow areas that may lead to inefficiencies. ▪ Automated Updates and Rollbacks: Kubernetes is self-healing: it can update the system automatically, and if there is any problem it can revert the changes. This capability is to make calls necessary to update the system so that it will always be up-to-date but without affecting its uptime or service. 2.2.11. Git Figure 33 - Git logo Git is one of the most popular distributed version control systems used by software engineers employed to respond for changes and synchronizing among developers. BDS uses Git to address basic components of efficient software development flowing in a well-organized and coordinated manner at Oracle Analytics Cloud. Using Git, BDS engineers can: ▪ Track Changes: This presented engineers with an avenue of documenting changes made in the codebase where Git provides users with the history recorded by the changes made. It also aids in identifying the developmental history of the code and ensure that one can easily go back to the earlier versions in case a need arises. ▪ Collaborate Efficiently: Branching and merging capability are standard in Git; they allow several engineers to collaborate on various features or the resolution of different issues at once by working on other branches. After the changes have been made, they can be placed back into a master branch containing the main code base. ▪ Manage Code Versions: It also lets you have the different branches for developments, testing, and conducting production. It also assists in effectively managing and stabilizing hockey stick production while continuing research and development as well as testing in the background. ▪ Enhance Code Quality: BDS engineers can check code reviews while integrating CI/CD utilities into the environment to avoid deployments of poor quality code through Git. ▪ Facilitate Remote Work: Because Git is a distributed system , engineers can be in any location while contributing towards the code base hence enhances collaboration with staff who may be working from remote locations. In conclusion, Git is a central and indispensable tool in the development lifecycle at BDS due to its powerful capabilities to manage versioning and facilitate collaborative work while maintaining code quality. This makes it easier for BDS engineers to achieve the goals of their company by providing users with efficient and dependable software. 2.2.12. Integrated Development Environments At Oracle Analytics Cloud, engineers use IDEs to make coding easier and more efficient. Two popular IDEs in use are IntelliJ IDEA and PyCharm, both made by JetBrains. IntelliJ IDEA Figure 34 - IntelliJ Logo IntelliJ IDEA is mainly used for Java development. engineers like it because: ▪ Smart Suggestions: It helps by suggesting code as you type, which speeds up writing and reduces errors. ▪ Easy Refactoring: It has tools to quickly improve and clean up code without breaking it. ▪ Powerful Debugger: It lets engineers find and fix problems in their code by running it stepby- step. ▪ Built-in Tools: IntelliJ IDEA includes tools for version control, managing databases, and automating builds, all in one place. ▪ User-Friendly: Its interface is easy to use and can be customized to fit personal preferences. 4. Conclusion In this chapter, we presented the problem statement and the main objectives of the project. We examined the technical foundations of Oracle Big Data Service (BDS), including its development process, the technologies used, and the tools adopted by engineers. We also explained how these elements work together to ensure a smooth, efficient, and high-performance
chapters.Chapter 4: Project Implementation: 1. Introduction Having thoroughly examined the requirements and refined the solutions for connecting to the IDL and running Trino as a runtime within the IDL, it is now time to transition into the practical implementation phase. This section outlines the initial steps taken in updating our wrapper, including upgrading it to match the latest version of Trino. As this report is being written midway through my internship, it is important to note that the project is still ongoing, with several tasks currently in progress. Additionally, future tasks and potential enhancements are also discussed in this section. 2. Trino And Lake Metastore Implementation 2.1 Trino Trino is an open-source distributed SQL query engine designed to query large data sets distributed over one or more heterogeneous data sources. Trino can query data lakes that contain a variety of file formats such as simple row-oriented CSV and JSON data files to more performant open column-oriented data file formats like ORC or Parquet residing on different storage systems like HDFS, AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage using the Hive and Iceberg table formats. Trino also has the ability to run federated queries that query tables in different data sources such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, Cassandra,Kafka, MongoDB and Elasticsearch. Trino is released under the Apache License At the start of my internship, my mentor recommended a very powerful book to help me learn about Trino. The O’Reilly book, Trino: The Definitive Guide, is an excellent resource that provides a solid understanding of Trino’s architecture, features, and usage. It has been especially helpful in deepening my knowledge of how Trino works and how to use it effectively. Query using Trino Figure 35 - query with Trino Trino Architecture: Figure 36 - Trino cluster 2.2 TrinoWrraper Overview The TrinoWrapper is composed of seven Java classes, each with its own specific role. Figure 37 - Trino-hive module Figure 38 - Lake implementation 1. OracleLakeMetastoreModule • Role: A Guice module that configures bindings for the Oracle Lake metastore. • Key Actions: o Binds OracleLakeHiveMetastoreFactory as the factory for creating metastore instances. o Binds OracleLakeHiveMetastoreConfig to load configuration (e.g., from hive.properties). • Dependency: Installed by HiveMetastoreModule when hive.metastore=oraclelake. 2. OracleLakeHiveMetastoreConfig • Role: Stores configuration properties for the Oracle Lake metastore (e.g., connection URIs, credentials). • Usage: Injected into OracleLakeHiveMetastoreFactory to initialize the metastore. 3. OracleLakeHiveMetastoreFactory • Role: Implements HiveMetastoreFactory to create instances of OracleLakeMetastore. • Key Methods: o createMetastore(): Initializes OracleLakeMetastore with config and authentication. • Dependencies: o Requires OracleLakeHiveMetastoreConfig for settings. 4. OracleLakeMetastore • Role: Core implementation of the HiveMetastore interface for Oracle Lake. • Key Responsibilities: o Overrides Hive metastore methods like getDatabase, getTable, createTable to interact with Oracle Lake’s metadata storage. o Uses TrinoConverter to translate between Trino and Oracle Lake metadata formats. • Interface Compliance: Must adhere to HiveMetastore (e.g., handle partitions, table schemas). 5. OracleLakeAuthenticationProvider • Role: Handles authentication (e.g., Kerberos, OAuth) for Oracle Lake connections. • Usage: Called by OracleLakeHiveMetastoreFactory to authenticate before creating the metastore. • Example: Validates credentials from OracleLakeHiveMetastoreConfig. 6. OracleLakeConstants • Role: Defines constants (e.g., property keys, default values) used across the module. public static final String CONFIG_KEY_OCI_METASTORE_URI = "oci.metastore.uris"; public static final String DEFAULT_CATALOG_NAME = "oraclelake"; 7. TrinoConverter • Role: Converts metadata between Trino’s internal format and Oracle Lake’s native format. • Key Methods: o toTrinoDatabase(): Maps Oracle Lake DB metadata to Trino’s Database class. o fromTrinoTable(): Converts Trino Table metadata to Oracle Lake’s format. • Usage: Used by OracleLakeMetastore during metadata operations. Figure 39 – TrinoWrapper Diagram class 2.3 Design OCI Metastore Plugin In this section, we present the sequence diagram that illustrates how the Lake implementation is invoked and utilized within Trino when integrating with the OCI Metastore Plugin. This diagram highlights the interaction between key components and demonstrates the flow of requests from Trino to the OCI Lake Metastore, showcasing how metadata operations are handled under the hood. Figure 40 - sequence diagram lake Flow fo Execution: • TrinoServer : the main entry point that starts and initializes the Trino server. It loads configurations, sets up the server environment, and initializes necessary modules. • ServerMainModule : this is the primary Guice module that installs and configures essential modules for Trino. It installs HiveMetastoreModule (or similar metastore-related modules) to define how Trino interacts with metastores. • HiveMetastoreModule : This module binds metastore implementations based on configuration. It maps metastore types (e.g., "oraclelake") to their respective modules. This tells Trino that when hive.metastore=oraclelake is set in the config, it should use OracleLakeMetastoreModule. • OracleLakeMetastoreModule : A Guice module that defines bindings specific to the Oracle Lake Metastore. It binds: OracleLakeHiveMetastoreFactory →Responsible for creating instances of OracleLakeMetastore. OracleLakeHiveMetastoreConfig → Loads and stores configuration properties (e.g., from hive.properties). • OracleLakeHiveMetastoreFactory : Implements the factory pattern to create and manage instances of OracleLakeMetastore. Handles initialization (e.g., connection pooling, authentication) for the metastore. • OracleLakeHiveMetastoreConfig : A configuration class that reads and validates settings from hive.properties. • OracleLakeMetastore : Your custom implementation of a Hive-compatible metastore for Oracle Lake. Overrides methods like getDatabase, getTable, and createTable to interact with Oracle Lake’s metadata storage. 2.4 Trino Version Upgrade: From 389 to 468 : A key milestone in this POC was updating our custom trinoWrapper, an abstraction layer enabling seamless interaction with the Trino query engine. The challenge lay in adapting it from Trino v389 (used in Oracle Big Data Service) to a more recent version like v468, which includes significant changes and enhancements. Key Areas of Change Requiring trinoWrapper Adaptation: 1. Client API and SPI Changes Trino v468 introduced breaking changes in client libraries and internal SPIs (e.g., connectors, event listeners). Impact: The wrapper’s connection setup, query execution, metadata handling, and result processing logic were updated to reflect these changes. 2. Configuration and Property Management New versions added or deprecated configuration parameters. Impact: The wrapper was refactored to support new properties, handle deprecated ones, and expose relevant options to downstream applications. 3. SQL Syntax and Feature Enhancements Trino added new SQL capabilities, functions, and error codes. Impact: Error handling and result interpretation logic in the wrapper need to be adjusted to align with updated SQL behavior. 4. Performance and Optimizer Changes Improvements to the query planner affected query execution characteristics. Impact: The wrapper's monitoring and logging features were reviewed to ensure compatibility with new optimization behaviors. 5. Dependency Management Trino's dependency upgrades (e.g., Guava, Jackson) required careful conflict resolution. Impact: Dependencies were aligned to prevent runtime issues and ensure compatibility. Outcome: Successfully adapting the trinoWrapper to Trino v468 ,It ensures robust, secure, and performant integration with the modern Trino engine, laying the foundation for its adoption within the Oracle Intelligent Data Lake ecosystem. Example: Problem 1. Direct use of org.apache.hadoop.hive.metastore.api tightly coupled Trino's codebase to Hive's Thrift API, making it vulnerable to changes in Hive's implementation. 2. Dependency on Hive's classes complicated maintenance and caused potential version conflicts when Hive's Thrift API evolved. Solution 1. Trino introduced io.trino.hive.thrift.metastore as a wrapper around Hive's Thrift classes to abstract and decouple its internal logic from Hive's implementation. 2. The conversion to Hive's format (org.apache.hadoop.hive.metastore.api) is now needed. And we will do this conversion by the use of Apache Thrift serialization and deserialization: Figure 41 - Apache Thrift S-D Class: ThriftObjectConverter Package: io.trino.plugin.hive.metastore.oracle.lake Purpose: The ThriftObjectConverter class provides utility methods to convert between Thrift-based data structures used by Trino's Hive metastore and the Apache Hive metastore API. It leverages Apache Thrift serialization and deserialization to enable seamless conversion of complex objects between Trino and Hive representations. Key Features: • Uses TSerializer and TDeserializer with a TBinaryProtocol for binary encoding and decoding of Thrift objects. • Provides a generic convert method to convert any Thrift object of type S to another Thrift type T using serialization and deserialization. • Supplies convenience methods for specific conversions between Trino and Hive metastore objects. Figure 43 - ThriftObjectConverter in IntelliJ Example: CreateTable API In this example, I will explain how the createTable Api updated: Figure 44 - – old createTable API Figure 45 - new createTable API In this API, I used the ThriftObjectConverter to convert metadata objects from Trino's format (io.trino.hive.thrift.metastore) to Hive's native format (org.apache.hadoop.hive.metastore.api). This conversion is essential for enabling seamless interoperability between Trino and Hive metastore services, allowing Trino to interact with Hive-compatible components using standardized metadata structures 2.5. learn OKE and trino operator concepts 2.4.1 Oracle Kubernetes engine: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Kubernetes Engine is a fully-managed, scalable, and highly available service that you can use to deploy your containerized applications to the cloud. Use Kubernetes Engine (also known as Container Engine for Kubernetes, and sometimes abbreviated to just OKE) when your development team wants to reliably build, deploy, and manage cloud- native applications. Figure 46 - Oracle OKE arch In my case, I provisioned an Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) cluster in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) to manage and orchestrate containerized applications. After setting up the OKE environment, I deployed my container images into the cluster for testing and validation. As part of this process, I integrated the Trino Operator within the OKE cluster, which simplified the deployment and management of Trino instances. By using the operator, I was able to define Trino deployments declaratively and efficiently manage scaling, configuration, and lifecycle operations. This setup allowed me to test my images in a production-like Kubernetes environment, ensuring they were running correctly with all necessary dependencies, and verifying the behavior of Trino when integrated with other components such as the Hive metastore and object storage. The TrinoOperator plays a crucial role in managing and orchestrating Trino deployments within a Kubernetes environment. It simplifies the process of running Trino by handling tasks such as configuring catalogs, managing cluster components (coordinator and workers), and ensuring high availability. In my case, I used the TrinoOperator to deploy and run my Trino images efficiently. This allowed me to set up and manage Trino instances for testing purposes, including running TPC-H queries and validating the integration of custom plugins like the OCI Metastore Plugin. The operator streamlined the process, making it easier to conduct my experiments and ensure a stable testing environment. This operator was developed by an engineer on our team with strong expertise in DevOps. Figure 47 - Trino Operator screens as you can see here, I can easily configure my Trino deployment through the Trino Operator— including adding catalogs, setting properties, and customizing configurations as needed. With the use of trino operator and oke : First I need to acces the OKE using OCI CLI. Create operator image: ismail@Ismails-MacBook-Pro trino-operator % make docker -build IMG=”iad.ocir.io/idpbwtq1b3ta/ismail-cr/trinopcluster:v0.0.1” Pushing image to container registry: : (base) ismail@Ismails-MacBook-Pro trino-operator % make docker -push IMG=”iad.ocir.io/idpbuiugia/ismail-cr/trinopcluster:v0.0.1” Deploying Trino-Operator on Kubernetes cluster: : ismail@Ismails-MacBook-Pro trino-operator % make deploy IMG=”iad.ocir.io/idpbuiugia/ismail- cr/trinopcluster:v0.0.1” Create sample TrinoCluster(Custom Resource) instance : (base) ismail@Ismails-MacBook-Pro trino-operator % make docker -build IMG=kubectl create -f config/samples/bds_v1alpha1_trinocluster.yaml Validate Trino cluster is up & running (base) ismail@Ismails-MacBook-Pro trino-operator % kubectl get pods NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE trinocluster-sample-trino-coordinator 1/1 Running 0 45s trinocluster-sample-trino-worker 1/1 Running 0 43s trinocluster-sample-trino-worker 1/1 Running 0 43s 3. Trino Integrartion with IDL 3.1 Connection to IDL In this part, I will explain how we attempted to interact with the IDL (Interface Definition Language) endpoint. First of all, it’s important to note that the IDL service is not exposed to any non-IDL components, meaning we cannot directly access or invoke the HMS (Hive Metastore) use the DCAT JAR client for the metastore, which provides the necessary client-side implementation for communicating with the metastore. We then tried to integrate this JAR into our Trino wrapper. To enable communication, we also had to request whitelisting for this integration to be accepted by the system. By following this approach — using the DCAT client and securing the required permissions — we were able to overcome the access restrictions and move closer to achieving our goal of connecting Trino to the HMS via the IDL service. Figure 48 - how we try to connect to IDL 3.2 Adapting the Trino IDL extension layer The adaptation of the Trino IDL extension layer (on Trino 389) to support new interface-level changes from Lake and DCAT IDL upgrades proved to be the most technically challenging aspect of the migration. The core complexity stemmed from resolving deep dependency conflicts introduced by incompatible transitive Key Challenges Addressed: • Identified and resolved 60+ interface incompatibilities in the extension layer where method signatures and class structures had fundamentally changed between versions • Performed exhaustive dependency tree analysis to isolate version conflicts propagating through multiple layers • Implemented strategic exclusions and version overrides to establish consistency across the dependency graph The resolution required careful analysis of 60+ transitive dependencies and their compatibility matrices, making this the most complex part of the upgrade process. The solution maintains backward compatibility while enabling new DCAT functionality through precise version pinning and exclusion rules. 4. Future Tasks As the project continues to progress, it's important to note that the implementation is ongoing. The upcoming tasks focus on enhancing the system's capabilities and validating its performance in a production-like environment. One of the key future steps involves planning and deploying a new Trino cluster within the Corp tenancy, ensuring it is properly connected to the whitelisted IDL catalog and Oracle Lake endpoints. This setup will serve as the foundation for further testing and validation. Additional tasks that are yet to be started include the full-scale execution of performance benchmarks. The final milestone will consist of running the TPC-DS benchmark using comparable resources and dataset configurations across both platforms. This will allow us to generate a detailed performance comparison between the Dataflow Spark runtime and the Trino runtime, helping to evaluate efficiency, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. 5. Conclusion This chapter outlines the successful development and enhancement of the TrinoWrapper and the integration of IDL-based connectivity with the Hive Metastore. These improvements were central to my internship mission and contributed meaningfully to Oracle’s efforts in advancing Trino as a powerful distributed SQL engine. The implemented Proof of Concept (PoC) represents a significant step forward in improving interoperability between Trino and Oracle’s data infrastructure, particularly within the Intelligent Data Lake (IDL) ecosystem. It simplifies Hive integration, reduces metadata retrieval latency, and enhances overall query performance. As the project progresses, future efforts will focus on enhancing the system’s capabilities and validating its performance in a production-like environment. A key upcoming task includes deploying a new Trino cluster within the Corp tenancy, connected to the whitelisted IDL catalog and Oracle Lake endpoints. In addition, performance benchmarking—particularly the execution of TPC-DS comparisons between Dataflow Spark and Trino runtimes—will serve as a critical step in assessing efficiency, scalability, and cost-effectiveness

abstract: Ce rapport présente le résultat de mon projet de fin d’études, qui portait sur la valida- tion de l’intégrité des opérations d’aplatissement d’arbres dans les systèmes d’entreprise. Dans de nombreuses applications à grande échelle, les données hiérarchiques doivent être transformées en structures plates et tabulaires pour leur traitement, analyse ou stockage. Il est crucial que cette transformation préserve la précision et la structure des données originales. L’objectif principal du projet était de développer un cadre de validation automatisé pour vérifier la correction des données d’arbres aplaties. Ce cadre évalue divers aspects struc- turels de la transformation, notamment les relations entre nœuds, la profondeur de la hiérarchie, et la cohérence entre différentes stratégies d’aplatissement. Une approche modulaire et réutilisable a été adoptée, permettant l’intégration du système de validation dans les flux de travail existants et son adaptation à plusieurs cas d’usage. La solution a été conçue en tenant compte de la maintenabilité et de la scalabilité, afin de pouvoir gérer des structures d’arbres complexes et de grands jeux de données. En conclusion, ce projet souligne l’importance des outils de validation automatisés pour garantir l’intégrité des données lors des transformations structurelles, contribuant ainsi à une plus grande fiabilité des pipelines de données en entreprise. Mots-clés : Arbre, Aplatissement, Validation de l’aplatissement, Données hiérarchiques
